subtopic_detail: managing excessive fluid intake causing a falling sodium in a long stay inpatient
stem:
You are the doctor on a psychiatric inpatient unit. A 38-year-old man with chronic schizophrenia, admitted six weeks ago and stable on olanzapine, has had two witnessed generalised seizures today. Nursing staff report he drinks continuously from the ward taps and bathroom, and that he has been found filling bottles overnight. His weight recorded at 7 am was 78 kg and at 4 pm today was 83 kg.

He is drowsy and confused post-ictally. Pulse rate 88 per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. He is clinically euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes and no oedema. Sodium is 118 mmol/L (135 to 145), serum osmolality 248 mosmol/kg (275 to 295), urine osmolality 62 mosmol/kg and urine sodium 12 mmol/L. Thyroid function and morning cortisol are within normal limits and he takes no diuretic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy and confused post-ictally; clinically euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes and no oedema; 5 kg weight gain across a single day
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L (135 to 145); serum osmolality 248 mosmol/kg (275 to 295); urine osmolality 62 mosmol/kg; urine sodium 12 mmol/L; thyroid function and morning cortisol within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence fluid restriction alone at 800 mL per day and recheck the sodium and serum osmolality in the morning
Commence an infusion of sodium chloride 0.9 per cent at 125 mL per hour and recheck the sodium every four hours
Cease the olanzapine and commence fluid restriction, attributing the disturbance to antipsychotic inappropriate antidiuresis
Commence tolvaptan to promote free water excretion and monitor the rate of sodium correction with six hourly measurements
Give hypertonic sodium chloride 3 per cent in small boluses for the seizures, then restrict fluid with target weight monitoring

subtopic_detail: priorities of the health screen performed on reception into a custodial facility
stem:
You are the doctor performing reception health screening at a metropolitan remand centre. A 26-year-old man was received two hours ago, charged with serious offences following an incident yesterday. He has never been in custody before. He is quiet, makes little eye contact and gives brief answers.

He tells you he last used intravenous methamphetamine three days ago and drinks about fifteen standard drinks daily, with his last drink yesterday morning. He was prescribed sertraline by a general practitioner four months ago but has not taken it for two weeks. He says his partner has ended the relationship since his arrest and that he has let everybody down. When you ask directly, he says he has thought about hanging himself but has no current plan. He has a fine tremor and is diaphoretic. Pulse rate 104 per minute, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 per minute, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor of outstretched hands; diaphoresis; injection marks in left antecubital fossa; no confusion or hallucinations; restricted affect with limited eye contact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Document that he has no current plan, provide crisis contact information, and arrange routine review at the next scheduled clinic
Place him on enhanced observation with a safe cell, commence symptom triggered withdrawal management, and restart his antidepressant
Restart sertraline, arrange a mental health team review within seven days, and place him in standard shared accommodation
Prescribe a fixed dose reducing diazepam regimen for alcohol withdrawal and review his mental state once the withdrawal has resolved
Transfer him to the emergency department of the nearest hospital for medical assessment of his withdrawal and mental state

subtopic_detail: recognising an inherited neurodegenerative cause of personality change with involuntary movements
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 41-year-old man referred by his general practitioner with depression and anger outbursts. Over two years his wife has noticed he has become uncharacteristically irritable, indifferent to his children's activities and unable to organise the household paperwork he used to manage. He was dismissed from work for errors. He denies feeling sad and says everyone else has changed, not him.

His father died at 52 in a psychiatric hospital with what the family were told was alcoholic dementia. On examination he is fidgety, with brief irregular movements of the fingers and face that he incorporates into apparently purposeful gestures. He cannot sustain tongue protrusion or a steady handgrip. Saccadic eye movements are slow to initiate. He scores poorly on verbal fluency and the trail making test but recall with cueing is preserved. Thyroid function, copper studies, syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology and vitamin B12 are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Brief irregular non-repetitive movements of fingers and face incorporated into voluntary gestures; unable to sustain tongue protrusion or maintain grip; slowed saccade initiation; impaired verbal fluency and set shifting with preserved cued recall
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, caeruloplasmin and copper studies, syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Tardive dyskinesia arising from previously prescribed antipsychotic medication, with an associated depressive syndrome
Wilson disease with neuropsychiatric presentation and an associated movement disorder in early middle age
Alcohol related brain injury producing frontal executive dysfunction, amnesia and a cerebellar movement disturbance
Huntington disease presenting with personality change, executive impairment and early involuntary movements
Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia with disinhibition, apathy and loss of executive planning capacity

subtopic_detail: responding to nocturnal eating with no recall in a woman taking a hypnotic for insomnia
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 44-year-old woman who has been taking zolpidem 10 mg at night for eight months for insomnia after a workplace restructure. She comes today because she is frightened. On four occasions in the past month her husband has found her in the kitchen at 2 am eating frozen food and uncooked pasta, and once she had turned on the stove. She has no memory of any of it.

She has gained 6 kg since starting the medication and has been finding food wrappers in her bed. She drinks no alcohol. Her mood is reasonable, she denies binge eating or purging while awake, and she has never restricted her intake or felt driven to compensate for eating. She has no history of parasomnia in childhood. Her thyroid function, glycated haemoglobin, full blood count and iron studies are within normal limits, and she takes no other medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 29 kg/m2 having risen from 27 kg/m2; mental state examination unremarkable with euthymic mood and no preoccupation with weight or shape
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, glycated haemoglobin, full blood count and iron studies within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the zolpidem with a planned taper and refer her for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia with home safety advice
Reduce the zolpidem to 5 mg at night and review whether the nocturnal episodes continue over the following month
Refer her for eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy for probable night eating syndrome with nocturnal awakenings
Switch her to temazepam at night, since benzodiazepines are not associated with this class of adverse effect
Arrange overnight polysomnography and continue the current dose until the study has clarified the nature of the episodes

subtopic_detail: responding to a request for opioid dose escalation in long term non-cancer pain with sedative co-prescription
stem:
You are the doctor in a combined pain and mental health clinic seeing a 53-year-old former warehouse worker with nine years of low back pain following a lifting injury. He takes oxycodone modified release 80 mg twice daily, immediate release oxycodone 10 mg up to four times daily, diazepam 10 mg at night for sleep and pregabalin 300 mg twice daily.

His pain scores have risen over the last year despite two dose increases, and he now describes pain spreading to areas that were previously unaffected and finds even light touch on his back uncomfortable. He has become withdrawn, sleeps poorly and has stopped his hydrotherapy. He denies using illicit drugs and his prescription monitoring record shows no early dispensing or multiple prescribers. Magnetic resonance imaging eighteen months ago showed degenerative change without nerve root compression. His morning testosterone is low, he is constipated, and he asks you today to increase the oxycodone again.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Diffuse tenderness extending beyond the original injury site; allodynia to light touch over the lumbar region; no focal neurological deficit; normal straight leg raise
data_table.Investigations: Magnetic resonance imaging 18 months ago shows degenerative change without nerve root compression; morning testosterone low; prescription monitoring record shows no early dispensing or multiple prescribers

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Repeat the magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine and defer any medication change until the new images are reviewed
Increase the oxycodone modified release dose as requested and review his pain scores and function again in four weeks
Begin a slow supervised opioid taper with a benzodiazepine taper, add duloxetine, and restart active rehabilitation with psychological support
Rotate the oxycodone to an equianalgesic dose of methadone and maintain the diazepam and pregabalin at their current doses
Stop all opioids abruptly today, provide symptomatic withdrawal medication, and review him in the clinic in one week

subtopic_detail: deciding whether to raise or lower corticosteroid when psychosis emerges during treatment of an autoimmune disease
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see a 24-year-old woman on the renal ward. She was admitted eleven days ago with systemic lupus erythematosus and biopsy proven class IV nephritis, and was commenced on prednisolone 60 mg daily nine days ago after three pulses of methylprednisolone.

Over the last two days she has become perplexed, believes the nursing staff are substituting her medication, and has been seen responding to voices. Her treating team is divided between reducing the corticosteroid and increasing it. She has a new right sided pronator drift and two brief episodes of right arm jerking witnessed overnight. Temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius with other vital signs within normal limits. Complement C3 and C4 are falling, double stranded deoxyribonucleic acid antibody titre is rising, and her creatinine has risen from 118 to 164 micromol/L (45 to 90). Cerebrospinal fluid shows 22 lymphocytes per microlitre with a raised protein, a normal glucose and a negative Gram stain.

data_table.Vital signs: Temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius with pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Perplexed with persecutory beliefs and auditory hallucinations; new right sided pronator drift; two witnessed brief episodes of right arm jerking; no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: Complement C3 and C4 falling; double stranded deoxyribonucleic acid antibody titre rising; creatinine risen from 118 to 164 micromol/L (45 to 90); cerebrospinal fluid 22 lymphocytes per microlitre with raised protein, normal glucose and negative Gram stain

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reduce the prednisolone dose progressively and commence olanzapine, attributing the presentation to corticosteroid induced psychosis
Cease the corticosteroid entirely and commence intravenous aciclovir empirically for suspected herpes simplex encephalitis
Commence haloperidol and lorazepam for the psychotic symptoms and defer any change to her immunosuppressive regimen
Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy for the psychotic presentation and continue her current corticosteroid dose unchanged
Escalate immunosuppression after excluding infection, and treat the psychotic symptoms symptomatically while monitoring neurologically

subtopic_detail: escalating hypnotic use for chronic insomnia with no depressive, respiratory or movement disorder contributors
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 52-year-old accountant who has had eight months of waking at 2 am and lying awake for two hours. Another doctor at the practice started zopiclone 7.5 mg five months ago for short term use.

She now takes it every night, says it no longer works as well, and is frightened of nights without it. She scores 4 on the PHQ-9 and denies low mood, anhedonia or anxiety. Her partner reports no snoring and no witnessed pauses in breathing, and her body mass index is 24 kg/m2. She has no evening leg restlessness or urge to move, drinks one coffee before 9 am, and works standard daytime hours with no shift work.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Assessment: PHQ-9 score 4, no snoring or witnessed apnoeas reported by partner, body mass index 24 kg/m2, no restless legs symptoms, no shift work, caffeine limited to the morning
data_table.Medications: Zopiclone 7.5 mg nightly for five months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase zopiclone to 15 mg at night and review her again in four weeks
Switch to temazepam 10 mg nightly and continue it long term as required
Start mirtazapine 15 mg at night for its sedating effect on sleep onset
Begin cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia and taper the zopiclone
Order a diagnostic polysomnogram before making any change to treatment

subtopic_detail: inability to fall asleep before the early hours with normal sleep quality and duration when the schedule is unconstrained
stem:
You are the doctor in a youth health clinic seeing a 16-year-old boy brought by his mother because he is missing the first two periods at school most days.

He says he lies awake until 2 or 3 am no matter what time he goes to bed, then cannot be woken at 7 am and feels drugged for hours. In the school holidays he goes to sleep at about 2 am, sleeps until 11 am, and wakes refreshed with good energy and concentration for the rest of the day. He is not sad, still plays basketball, sees friends, and scores 12 on the Kessler 10. He uses his phone in bed until he falls asleep. He takes no medication and does not use alcohol or other drugs.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Assessment: Kessler 10 score 12, sleep onset consistently 2 to 3 am, sleep duration 8 to 9 hours and refreshing when the schedule is unconstrained, no snoring, no daytime naps, no substance use
data_table.Examination: Physical examination unremarkable, mood reactive with normal affect

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start temazepam at night for two weeks to re-establish a sleep pattern
Refer for an overnight sleep study before making any treatment decision
Start sertraline as the pattern suggests an underlying depressive illness
Advise a later school start and no other change to his routine for now
Use timed low dose melatonin in the early evening with morning bright light

subtopic_detail: a newly added non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug in an older woman established on a serotonergic antidepressant
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 67-year-old woman who has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for two years with a good response and no residual depressive symptoms.

At an appointment last week another doctor started regular naproxen 500 mg twice daily for painful knee osteoarthritis, and she has taken it for six days. She had intermittent dyspepsia two years ago, when testing for Helicobacter pylori was negative and an endoscopy was normal. She takes no other regular medication, in particular no aspirin, anticoagulant or acid suppressing drug. She has no melaena, no vomiting and no abdominal pain today, and she asks whether the two tablets are safe together.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 100 mg daily for two years, naproxen 500 mg twice daily started six days ago, no aspirin, anticoagulant or proton pump inhibitor
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 131 g/L (115-155), creatinine 71 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 74 mL/min/1.73m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop oral naproxen and use a topical anti-inflammatory with paracetamol
Continue naproxen and add a proton pump inhibitor for gastric protection
Continue naproxen and switch sertraline to another drug of the same class
Continue both drugs and check a full blood count every three months instead
Stop sertraline and continue naproxen, reviewing her mood again in a month

subtopic_detail: hyperactivity and learning difficulty in a child with documented heavy prenatal alcohol exposure and three sentinel facial features
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a community clinic seeing a 6-year-old boy who has been in foster care since he was two. His teacher reports that he cannot stay in his seat, interrupts constantly, and is two years behind in reading.

His case file documents that his birth mother drank heavily throughout the pregnancy, with several hospital presentations for intoxication. His foster carers describe poor impulse control, difficulty following two step instructions, no sense of danger around traffic, and trouble with money and time concepts. On examination his palpebral fissures are short, the philtrum is smooth and the upper lip is thin. His height and weight are on the 10th centile and his head circumference is on the 5th. Hearing and vision screening at school entry were normal.

data_table.Examination: Short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border of the upper lip, height and weight on the 10th centile, head circumference on the 5th centile
data_table.History: Documented heavy prenatal alcohol exposure, foster placement since age 2, no reported head injury or seizures
data_table.Assessment: School entry hearing and vision screening normal, reading two years below year level

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start methylphenidate now and review the response in four weeks
Refer for multidisciplinary neurodevelopmental assessment across domains
Arrange genetic microarray testing and defer any other assessment
Reassure the carers that the features will improve with a stable placement
Refer for hearing and vision testing alone and review in six months

subtopic_detail: five days without a bowel motion and abdominal distension in a man established on clozapine
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community mental health team. A 34-year-old man with schizophrenia has taken clozapine 450 mg daily for three years with an excellent response and no admissions.

At his clozapine clinic visit today he mentions that he has not opened his bowels for five days, which he says has been building up for a couple of months, and that his belly feels tight. He has no vomiting and is still eating. His abdomen is mildly distended and tympanic with bowel sounds present and no guarding or rebound. He takes no laxative and no anticholinergic medication. His neutrophil count today is within the normal range and he is afebrile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen mildly distended and tympanic, bowel sounds present, no guarding or rebound tenderness, no palpable mass
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 3.4 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), C-reactive protein 4 mg/L (<5), electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Add an anticholinergic agent to control the associated hypersalivation
Reduce the clozapine dose by half and review the bowels in one week
Start macrogol now and arrange an abdominal radiograph the same day
Advise increased dietary fibre and fluids and review again in one week
Arrange an outpatient colonoscopy within the next four to six weeks

subtopic_detail: persistent dense anterograde memory impairment with confabulation three months after a treated thiamine deficient encephalopathy
stem:
You are the doctor at a residential rehabilitation service reviewing a 54-year-old man who has been abstinent from alcohol for three months. He drank a bottle of spirits daily for 30 years.

Three months ago he was admitted with unsteadiness and confusion and treated with high dose parenteral thiamine, after which his eye movements and gait recovered. He is now alert, attentive and oriented to place and person, and he can hold a conversation and repeat a list immediately. He cannot recall any of three words after five minutes, does not remember the fire drill yesterday, and fills the gaps with detailed accounts of a fishing trip that staff confirm did not happen. His performance has been unchanged across three assessments over the last eight weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Assessment: Attention and immediate registration intact, dense anterograde amnesia with confabulation, no fluctuation in conscious level, no ophthalmoplegia or ataxia, performance stable across three assessments over 8 weeks
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and B12 within normal limits, magnetic resonance imaging showing mamillary body atrophy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start donepezil and review his cognition again in three months
Start an antipsychotic to treat the confabulated accounts he gives
Arrange further parenteral thiamine for another four week course
Continue oral thiamine and arrange a functional assessment for support
Repeat cognitive testing in two years before any further care planning

subtopic_detail: request for a cannabis prescription for generalised anxiety before any evidence based treatment has been tried
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29-year-old graphic designer who describes two years of constant worry about work, health and money, with muscle tension, irritability and difficulty concentrating on most days.

She has found an online clinic that advertises cannabis prescriptions for anxiety and asks you to write one so that she does not have to pay their fees. She has never had psychological therapy and has not tried an antidepressant, saying she has read that they are addictive. She drinks two standard drinks most evenings and does not use illicit substances. There is a family history of a psychotic illness in a maternal uncle. She works full time and her relationships are intact.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Assessment: GAD-7 score 15, no panic attacks, no depressive episode, no prior psychological therapy or antidepressant trial, alcohol 14 standard drinks per week, family history of psychotic illness
data_table.Examination: Physical examination unremarkable, thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Apply through the Special Access Scheme for a cannabidiol product now
Prescribe a short course of diazepam while she waits for an appointment
Refer her back to the online clinic that offered the cannabis prescription
Start an antipsychotic at low dose for the anxiety and review in a month
Offer structured psychological therapy first and decline the cannabis request

subtopic_detail: prolonged events with forced eye closure and no electroencephalographic change captured on telemetry in a woman on two antiseizure drugs
stem:
You are the registrar in a neuropsychiatry clinic seeing a 27-year-old woman referred after two years of events labelled as drug resistant epilepsy. She takes levetiracetam 1500 mg twice daily and lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily.

The events happen about three times a week and last 8 to 12 minutes, with thrashing of all four limbs that starts and stops repeatedly during the episode. Her eyes are held tightly closed and she resists attempts to open them. She is tearful afterwards but talking normally within a minute. Serum lactate measured 15 minutes after an event in the emergency department was normal. Five days of video telemetry captured three typical events with no change in the recording during any of them, and her magnetic resonance imaging is normal.

data_table.Assessment: Events 8 to 12 minutes with waxing and waning motor activity, forced eye closure with resistance, no postictal confusion, immediate return of speech
data_table.Investigations: Video telemetry over 5 days captured 3 typical events with no ictal or postictal electroencephalographic change, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain normal, post-event serum lactate within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Levetiracetam 1500 mg twice daily, lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Explain the diagnosis, refer for psychological therapy and withdraw the drugs
Add a third antiseizure medication and repeat the telemetry in six months
Refer for evaluation for epilepsy surgery given the drug resistant pattern
Tell her the events are not real and discharge her back to her own doctor
Start a benzodiazepine to be taken at the onset of each of the episodes

subtopic_detail: frequent brief crying episodes after a stroke with preserved mood, interest, sleep and appetite
stem:
You are the rehabilitation registrar reviewing a 71-year-old man six weeks after a left middle cerebral artery infarct that left him with mild dysarthria and a weak right hand.

His wife says he bursts into tears several times a day, often when a grandchild is mentioned or an advertisement comes on the television. The crying starts abruptly, lasts under a minute, and stops as suddenly as it began, after which he is embarrassed and says he was not feeling sad at all. He is sleeping well, eating well, works hard in physiotherapy, looks forward to visitors and laughs at jokes between the episodes. His PHQ-9 is 9, with 6 of those points coming from the crying and tearfulness items.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Assessment: PHQ-9 score 9 with most points from crying and tearfulness items, sleep and appetite preserved, interest and reactivity preserved, denies sadness during episodes
data_table.Examination: Mild dysarthria, right hand weakness with grade 4 power, no dysphagia, cognition intact on screening

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start mirtazapine at 30 mg at night and review his mood in six weeks
Start a low dose selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in two weeks
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for depression after the discharge
Reassure the family that no treatment is available for this symptom now
Start quetiapine at low dose at night to settle the emotional outbursts

subtopic_detail: new visual hallucinations with retained insight after a recent increase in dopaminergic therapy
stem:
You are the consultation liaison registrar asked to see a 74-year-old man with an eight year history of Parkinson disease who has been seeing small animals in his living room for three weeks.

He describes cats and possums that move along the skirting board in the evening, knows they are not really there, and is not frightened by them. His neurologist increased his pramipexole six weeks ago because of worsening tremor, and he also takes levodopa with carbidopa three times daily. He takes no anticholinergic or sedative drug. He is afebrile with no urinary symptoms, his midstream urine culture is negative, his inflammatory markers are normal and his cognitive screening score is 26 out of 30, unchanged from a year ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg lying and 112/68 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Assessment: Formed visual hallucinations with retained insight, no delusions, no fluctuation in attention, cognitive screening 26 out of 30 and unchanged from a year ago
data_table.Investigations: Midstream urine culture negative, C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5), sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Levodopa with carbidopa three times daily, pramipexole increased six weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.text: Start risperidone 0.5 mg at night and review the hallucinations in a week
Start haloperidol 0.5 mg as required for the visual hallucinations he has
Reduce then withdraw the dopamine agonist before considering other drugs
Stop levodopa first and continue the dopamine agonist at the same dose
Start donepezil and increase the levodopa dose to improve his mobility

subtopic_detail: egodystonic intrusive images of harming an infant with full insight and avoidance of care tasks
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29-year-old woman five weeks after the birth of her first baby. She asks her partner to take the baby out of the room, then tells you she has been having repeated images of drowning her daughter while bathing her.

She describes the images as horrifying and says they make her feel sick. She has stopped bathing the baby and hands her to her partner at bath time, and she has moved the kitchen knives to a high cupboard. She has no other unusual experiences, hears nothing, and does not believe anything is wrong with the baby or with herself beyond these thoughts. She sleeps when the baby sleeps, her mood is reactive, and she is breastfeeding successfully. Her Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score is 14 with a negative response to the self-harm item, and she is adamant she would never act on the images.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Assessment: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale 14 with negative self-harm item, intrusive images experienced as repugnant and alien, full insight, no hallucinations, no delusions, no elevated mood, sleep preserved
data_table.Examination: Infant thriving with appropriate weight gain, interaction warm and attuned, no neglect

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent psychiatric admission and separate her from the infant
Start an antipsychotic and review her again in the clinic in one week
Advise that another adult supervise all care until the thoughts stop
Arrange psychological therapy for the intrusive thoughts and keep them together
Refer to child protection services because of the risk to the infant

subtopic_detail: choosing between neuromodulation options when severe depression is accompanied by nihilistic delusions and food refusal
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 58-year-old man on the ward. He has had major depressive episodes before but nothing like this one, which has worsened over four months.

He has taken sertraline 200 mg daily for eight weeks and then venlafaxine 300 mg daily for eight weeks with lithium augmentation, both with documented adherence and no response. Over the last four days he has refused all food and fluid, saying his bowels have rotted away and that food would putrefy inside him. He speaks only in single words, moves slowly and has lost 8 kg in six weeks. His sodium is 149 mmol/L and his creatinine has risen from baseline. His wife is at the bedside and he has been assessed as lacking capacity to consent to treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Assessment: Psychomotor retardation, near mutism, nihilistic delusions about the bowel, refusing food and fluid for 4 days, weight loss 8 kg in 6 weeks, assessed as lacking capacity
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 149 mmol/L (135-145), urea 11.2 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110), thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Refer for a course of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation now
Add an atypical antipsychotic and review the response in four weeks
Start ketamine infusions as an outpatient over the next two weeks
Switch to a monoamine oxidase inhibitor after a two week washout period
Arrange electroconvulsive therapy after assessing capacity and consent

subtopic_detail: repetitive stealing of unneeded items preceded by tension and followed by relief in a financially secure adult
stem:
You are the psychiatrist assessing a 43-year-old primary school teacher referred by her lawyer after a second charge of shoplifting.

She has taken small items from supermarkets and chemists perhaps twice a month for four years. She describes mounting tension for an hour beforehand, a sense of release as she leaves the shop, then shame and self-disgust. She does not need the items, has never sold them, and keeps most of them in a cupboard or gives them to colleagues. Her household income is comfortable and her mortgage is nearly paid. She has not had periods of reduced sleep need, elevated mood, overspending or increased energy. She drinks two standard drinks a week, uses no other substances, and scores 29 out of 30 on cognitive screening. Her memory, language and social conduct at work are unchanged over the four years.

data_table.Assessment: Tension before and relief after each episode, items not needed and given away or stored, no financial hardship, no hypomanic or manic episodes, no substance use, cognitive screening 29 out of 30
data_table.Examination: Physical examination unremarkable, mood euthymic with congruent affect, no psychotic features

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting the urge to relief cycle
Start lithium as the behaviour represents an undiagnosed bipolar illness
Arrange brain imaging and refer for assessment of frontotemporal disease
Advise that this is a legal matter and no clinical assessment is needed
Start a stimulant as the pattern suggests an attention deficit disorder

subtopic_detail: planning the postpartum dose of an anticonvulsant mood stabiliser whose clearance rose through pregnancy
stem:
You are the perinatal psychiatry registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman at 34 weeks in her first pregnancy. She has bipolar II disorder and has been well for three years on lamotrigine 200 mg daily.

At 24 weeks she developed early depressive symptoms with poor sleep and rumination. A lamotrigine level taken then was about 40 per cent below her pre-pregnancy level, and the dose was increased in steps to 350 mg daily, after which her symptoms resolved and she has been well since. She plans to breastfeed and to birth at 39 weeks. She has had no rash and no other adverse effects. She asks what should happen to her tablets once the baby is born.

data_table.Assessment: Euthymic, sleeping adequately, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation, three years of stability before this pregnancy

Reduce towards the pre-pregnancy dose over the first two weeks after birth
Stop lamotrigine at the birth and restart it if symptoms recur afterwards
Halve the dose immediately after the birth and stop breastfeeding as well

subtopic_detail: multiple motor tics and one vocal tic for over a year in a nine year old with inattention
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 9-year-old boy referred by his general practitioner. His parents say he has been blinking hard and jerking his head to one side on and off since he was six, and that about a year ago he started making a repeated throat-clearing noise. The movements come in bouts, wax and wane in severity, and are worse when he is tired or excited.

He tells you he can feel a build-up like an itch just before each one and can hold them back for a short time in class, after which they come out in a burst at home. His teacher reports he is inattentive, loses his place and does not finish work, and this predates the vocal noise by two years. He has friends, enjoys swimming and is not being teased. The tics do not interfere with his handwriting or his sleep, and he says they do not bother him much. Neurological examination including gait, tone, power and coordination is normal, and he takes no medication and uses no substances.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Tic history: Multiple motor tics from age six and a vocal tic for one year, waxing and waning, worse with fatigue
data_table.Premonitory features: Describes a premonitory urge with temporary voluntary suppression followed by rebound
data_table.Functional impact: Handwriting, sleep and peer relationships unaffected, inattention predating the vocal tic by two years
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination including gait, tone, power and coordination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Start risperidone at a low dose and monitor his weight and prolactin level
Start clonidine at night and titrate the dose against the frequency of the tics
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before starting any treatment
Start methylphenidate and review whether the tics become more frequent later
Refer for comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics as first line therapy

subtopic_detail: a six year old who speaks freely at home but has not spoken at school for eight months
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old girl whose teacher has written asking for an assessment because the girl has not spoken a word at school since she started prep eight months ago. She nods, points and writes answers on a whiteboard, and completes written work at the expected standard.

Her parents say she chatters constantly at home, tells long stories to her grandmother on the phone, argues with her older brother and plays imaginative games with him involving reciprocal turn-taking and pretend. She spoke her first words at 11 months and put sentences together before she was two. At the surgery she sits close to her mother, makes brief eye contact with you, smiles at a joke and shakes her head when you ask a question, but does not speak. Her mother says she also goes silent with unfamiliar adults at the shops and at birthday parties. She passed her newborn hearing screen and has had no ear infections.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Speech pattern: Fluent age-appropriate speech at home, no speech at school for eight months, silent with unfamiliar adults
data_table.Developmental history: First words at 11 months, sentences before two years, passed newborn hearing screen
data_table.Social functioning: Reciprocal imaginative play with her brother, brief eye contact, smiles responsively in the consultation
data_table.Academic function: Written work at the expected standard, communicates by nodding, pointing and writing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for graded exposure therapy delivered jointly with her school
Refer for an autism spectrum diagnostic assessment before anything else
Start fluoxetine at a low dose and review her response in six weeks' time
Arrange audiology and formal speech pathology assessment of her language
Advise the school to reward each spoken word with additional playtime

subtopic_detail: inner restlessness and pacing two days after a dose increase in a previously settled inpatient
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on the ward. A 24-year-old man admitted eleven days ago with a first episode of psychosis had his risperidone increased from 2 mg to 4 mg daily two days ago because he was still describing persecutory beliefs. Nursing staff have called you because he has been pacing the corridor since early morning and cannot sit through a meal.

He tells you the feeling is in his legs and that he has to keep moving or it becomes unbearable, and that it is worse when he sits still and eases when he walks. He says it started yesterday and that it is not the voices. His speech is normal in rate and form, he is not distractible, and his persecutory beliefs are described in the same terms and with the same conviction as at admission. There is no tremor, no cogwheel rigidity and no dystonia. His pulse rate is 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air and temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Creatine kinase is 140 units/L (40-200).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Mental state: Normal speech rate and form, not distractible, persecutory beliefs unchanged in content and conviction
data_table.Subjective report: Restlessness localised to the legs, worse at rest and relieved by walking, onset the day after the dose increase
data_table.Neurological examination: No tremor, cogwheel rigidity or dystonia
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 140 units/L (40-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence diazepam and continue the current dose of risperidone unchanged
Reduce the risperidone dose and start propranolol for symptom relief
Increase the risperidone dose to treat the worsening psychotic agitation
Start benzatropine to treat the emerging extrapyramidal adverse effects
Add regular olanzapine at night in addition to his current treatment

subtopic_detail: six months of feeling detached from oneself with fully retained awareness that the experience is not real
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 23-year-old apprentice electrician referred by his general practitioner. He says that since a frightening episode six months ago, when his heart pounded and he thought he was dying, he has felt as though he is watching himself from a few feet away, like a character in a film rather than the person doing the living.

He describes his hands as looking like they belong to someone else and says the street outside looks flat and drained of colour, as though painted on a backdrop. He is emphatic that he knows none of this is actually true and that it is his perception that has changed rather than the world, and he finds that distinction frustrating rather than reassuring. It is present for most of the day, most days. He smoked cannabis heavily for two years and stopped seven months ago, before the symptoms began, and uses no other substance and no alcohol. He has no hallucinations, no delusional beliefs and no thought disorder, his mood is anxious rather than low, and physical examination, thyroid function and a recent electroencephalogram are all normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Core symptoms: Persistent detachment from self with a sense of observing oneself, and a flat drained quality to the surroundings
data_table.Reality testing: Fully intact, with explicit awareness that the altered perception does not reflect external reality
data_table.Substance history: Cannabis ceased seven months ago before symptom onset, no other substance or alcohol use
data_table.Mental state: No hallucinations, delusions or thought disorder, anxious rather than depressed mood
data_table.Investigations: Normal physical examination, thyroid function and electroencephalogram

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start a benzodiazepine to be taken whenever the detachment occurs
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before any treatment
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy addressing the symptoms
Start a low dose antipsychotic given the persistent unreal quality
Arrange electroencephalography to exclude temporal lobe epilepsy

subtopic_detail: recurrent replicative nightmares waking a veteran nightly despite improvement in his daytime symptoms
stem:
You are the psychiatrist reviewing a 44-year-old former soldier who has been taking sertraline 150 mg daily for nine months for post-traumatic stress disorder following a deployment. He has completed a course of trauma-focused therapy.

He tells you his daytime symptoms have improved substantially, with far fewer intrusive daytime images, less avoidance and a return to part-time work. What has not changed is that five or six nights a week he wakes between one and three in the morning from the same dream, which replays a specific incident almost exactly as it happened, and he then lies awake for two hours. His partner says he does not shout, thrash, kick or leave the bed, and neither of them has ever been injured during the night. He drinks no alcohol, uses no cannabis and takes no other medication. His mood is reactive, he is not suicidal, and his physical examination and blood tests including thyroid function are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Nightmare pattern: Replicative trauma-specific dreams waking him five or six nights weekly between 0100 and 0300 with two hours of subsequent wakefulness
data_table.Daytime symptoms: Substantially improved intrusions, reduced avoidance, returned to part-time work
data_table.Collateral from partner: No vocalisation, thrashing, kicking or leaving the bed, no injury to either partner
data_table.Treatment to date: Sertraline 150 mg daily for nine months, completed course of trauma-focused therapy
data_table.Investigations: Normal physical examination and blood tests including thyroid function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe nightly temazepam to consolidate sleep and reduce awakenings
Start quetiapine at night for its sedating and dream suppressing effect
Refer for polysomnography to assess for rapid eye movement behaviour
Refer for imagery rehearsal therapy targeting the recurrent nightmares
Increase the sertraline dose and review his sleep diary in six weeks

subtopic_detail: confusion and unsteadiness three weeks after starting an antidepressant in a woman of seventy nine
stem:
You are the general practitioner called to see a 79-year-old woman at home by her daughter, who says her mother has been muddled about the day of the week for three days and had a near fall in the kitchen. She was started on sertraline 50 mg daily three weeks ago for a depressive episode and reports her mood has lifted slightly.

Her other medications are amlodipine, atorvastatin and a thiazide she has taken for eight years without incident. She has had no cough, no urinary symptoms, no fever and no vomiting. On examination she is alert but disorientated to time, with normal power and no focal neurological signs, moist mucous membranes, no postural drop and no peripheral oedema. Her pulse rate is 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg lying and standing, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in air and temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. Sodium is 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), urea 3.1 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), serum osmolality 258 mmol/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 420 mmol/kg and urine sodium 52 mmol/L. Her sodium was 138 mmol/L eight weeks ago.

data_table.Electrolytes: Sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), urea 3.1 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90)
data_table.Osmolality studies: Serum osmolality 258 mmol/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 420 mmol/kg, urine sodium 52 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the sertraline and start hypertonic saline in a monitored setting
Halve the sertraline dose and repeat the sodium level again in two weeks
Switch her to mirtazapine today and recheck the sodium in three days' time
Start demeclocycline and continue the sertraline at her current daily dose
Cease the sertraline and commence fluid restriction with daily sodium checks

subtopic_detail: abdominal distension with absent bowel sounds in a man in his fourth year of clozapine treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 41-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia who has taken clozapine 500 mg daily for four years with good symptomatic control. Community staff report he has been off his food for five days, has vomited twice today and that his belly looks swollen.

He is drowsy but rousable and tells you his tummy has been aching and that he has not opened his bowels for nine days, which he says is not unusual for him. He takes no regular aperient. On examination the abdomen is grossly distended and tympanitic with generalised tenderness but no guarding, and bowel sounds are absent over four minutes of auscultation. There is no rigidity of the limbs and no tremor. His pulse rate is 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 102/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent in air and temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius. White cell count is 11.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with an absolute neutrophil count of 6.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), creatine kinase 180 units/L (40-200), lactate 3.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2) and creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 102/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent in air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Abdominal examination: Grossly distended tympanitic abdomen with generalised tenderness, no guarding, absent bowel sounds over four minutes
data_table.Neurological examination: Drowsy but rousable, no limb rigidity, no tremor
data_table.Bowel history: No bowel action for nine days, no regular aperient, two episodes of vomiting today
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 11.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), absolute neutrophil count 6.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), creatine kinase 180 units/L (40-200), lactate 3.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent abdominal imaging, withhold clozapine and involve the surgical team
Continue clozapine and start a stimulant laxative with review tomorrow morning
Check the clozapine level and reduce the dose by a quarter this same evening
Start an antiemetic and encourage oral fluids with a high fibre diet on the ward

subtopic_detail: partition delusions about a neighbour in a woman of seventy eight with intact cognition and normal imaging
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 78-year-old widow referred after she called the police three times in a fortnight. She believes the man in the next unit comes through the wall of her bedroom at night to move her belongings and put chemicals in her tea, and she has stopped drinking anything he might have reached.

She describes hearing his voice through the wall commenting on what she is doing. She lives alone, manages her own finances and medications accurately, cooks and shops independently, and her daughter confirms she has been sharp and organised until this began four months ago. On examination her Montreal Cognitive Assessment is 27 out of 30, attention and digit span are normal, and there is no fluctuation in her conscious level across a one hour interview. She has no visual hallucinations, no parkinsonism and no dream enactment. She wears two hearing aids that her daughter says stopped working months ago. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function, B12 and inflammatory markers are all normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Psychotic symptoms: Persecutory partition delusions involving the adjacent unit, auditory hallucinations through the wall, onset four months ago
data_table.Cognition: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 27 out of 30, normal attention and digit span, no fluctuation in conscious level
data_table.Neurological examination: No visual hallucinations, no parkinsonism, no dream enactment behaviour
data_table.Functional status: Independent with finances, medications, cooking and shopping

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy without any change to her medication
Start low dose amisulpride and arrange formal audiology assessment
Start donepezil and refer to the memory clinic for cognitive follow up
Treat as a delirium and screen for infection with cultures and further imaging

subtopic_detail: recurrent unexplained hypoglycaemia in a toddler that stops entirely during a supervised admission
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see the family of a 2-year-old girl admitted for the fourth time in three months with hypoglycaemic episodes. Each previous admission followed an ambulance call from home, and each time she recovered promptly and was discharged after a normal work-up.

During this nine-day admission, in which a nurse has been present at all cares and no food or drink has come from home, her glucose has remained between 4.2 and 6.8 mmol/L with no episodes. A sample taken during the last documented episode at home has now returned showing glucose 1.8 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), insulin 42 mIU/L, C-peptide less than 0.05 nmol/L (0.3-1.5) and beta-hydroxybutyrate suppressed. Cortisol and growth hormone responses were appropriate. Her mother, who trained as an enrolled nurse, has stayed at the bedside throughout, has asked repeatedly for further tests and has told several staff that a specialist interstate suspects a rare metabolic disorder. The treating team has been unable to verify that referral.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Inpatient course: Nine days with supervised cares and no external food, glucose 4.2 to 6.8 mmol/L with no episodes
data_table.Critical sample from home: Glucose 1.8 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), insulin 42 mIU/L, C-peptide less than 0.05 nmol/L (0.3-1.5), suppressed beta-hydroxybutyrate
data_table.Counter-regulatory testing: Appropriate cortisol and growth hormone responses
data_table.Collateral: Unverifiable account of an interstate specialist referral, repeated requests for further investigation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with a continuous glucose monitor and review her in one week
Offer the mother psychological therapy and arrange community follow up
Report to child protection services and keep the child in hospital
Arrange a supervised fast with paired insulin and cortisol sampling now
Refer to paediatric endocrinology for insulinoma localisation imaging

subtopic_detail: a specific threat against a named person disclosed in a session by a patient with a history of violence
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 38-year-old man in an outpatient clinic for the eighth time. He has been attending for help with anger and relationship difficulties following separation from his partner. He has two previous convictions for assault, the most recent four years ago.

Today he tells you that his former partner's new boyfriend, whom he names and whose workplace and shift pattern he describes, is going to be dealt with this week. He says he has bought a knife for the purpose and that he has driven past the workplace twice. He is calm, coherent and consistent as he describes this and he repeats it when you check you have understood. On mental state examination his speech is normal in rate and form, there is no evidence of any delusion, hallucination or thought disorder, his mood is euthymic with a congruent affect, and his cognition is intact. He has taken no alcohol or other substance today. He tells you he has said this to you in confidence and asks you not to repeat it.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Disclosure: Named intended victim with described workplace and shift pattern, weapon obtained, two reconnaissance visits, stated timeframe of this week
data_table.Mental state: Normal speech rate and form, no delusions, hallucinations or thought disorder, euthymic mood with congruent affect, intact cognition
data_table.Substance use: No alcohol or other substance taken today
data_table.History: Two previous convictions for assault, most recent four years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Arrange an involuntary admission under the mental health legislation today
Discuss the disclosure with the treating team at the next case meeting
Contact the medical defence organisation before taking any other action
Notify the police and take steps to warn the person who was named
Maintain confidentiality and document the disclosure fully in the case notes

subtopic_detail: repeated requests for rhinoplasty in a man who spends four hours a day checking mirrors
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 27-year-old man referred by a plastic surgeon who has declined to operate. He has had two previous rhinoplasties, the first at 21 and the second at 24, and says neither achieved what he wanted.

He tells you his nose is crooked and too wide and that people look at it on the train. He checks his profile in reflective surfaces for what he estimates as four hours a day, photographs his face from fixed angles each morning to compare, wears a cap pulled low and has stopped going to the gym or on dates. He resigned from a job requiring video meetings. He accepts that others tell him his nose looks normal but says they are being kind, and when you ask whether it is possible they are right he pauses and says probably not but he cannot be sure. There is no belief that he is being watched or persecuted, no hallucination, and no thought disorder. His mood is low with initial insomnia and he has thought about suicide if no surgeon will operate. The referring surgeon documented an anatomically normal nose.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Preoccupation: Estimated four hours daily of mirror checking and photographic comparison of a surgeon-documented normal nose
data_table.Functional impact: Resigned from work requiring video meetings, ceased gym attendance and dating, camouflages with a cap
data_table.Insight: Accepts reassurance is offered sincerely but cannot be certain his perception is mistaken
data_table.Mental state: Low mood with initial insomnia, no persecutory belief, hallucination or thought disorder, suicidal ideation contingent on surgical refusal
data_table.Surgical history: Two previous rhinoplasties at 21 and 24 with no relief of distress

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Support the referral for rhinoplasty given the distress that he describes
Start a low dose antipsychotic for the overvalued ideas about his nose
Refer for supportive counselling and review his progress again in six months
Start a benzodiazepine for the anxiety and reassess him after four weeks
Start a high dose selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor with cognitive therapy

subtopic_detail: raised corrected calcium with an unsuppressed parathyroid hormone after fifteen years of mood stabiliser treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatrist reviewing a 58-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has taken lithium for 15 years. She had three manic admissions before lithium was started and none since, and two previous attempts to switch her to other agents both ended in relapse within four months.

She feels well and has no bone pain, abdominal pain, polyuria or constipation. Her routine annual bloods show total calcium 2.72 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), albumin 32 g/L (35-50), phosphate 0.74 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), parathyroid hormone 7.2 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), lithium 0.72 mmol/L (0.60-0.80), creatinine 94 micromol/L (45-90) and estimated glomerular filtration rate 58 mL/min/1.73m2. Thyroid function is normal. A repeat set taken a fortnight later shows the same pattern. Her full blood count, liver function and serum protein electrophoresis are normal, and a myeloma screen is negative. She takes no thiazide, no calcium supplement and no vitamin D preparation, and she has had no recent immobilisation.

data_table.Calcium studies: Total calcium 2.72 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), albumin 32 g/L (35-50), phosphate 0.74 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), parathyroid hormone 7.2 pmol/L (1.6-6.9)

options.text: Refer for endocrine assessment and parathyroid imaging while continuing lithium

Start cinacalcet now and continue lithium at the current dose and interval

subtopic_detail: a prolonged repolarisation interval on opioid substitution therapy after a second drug was added
stem:
You are the addiction medicine registrar reviewing a 46-year-old man who has been stable on methadone 130 mg daily for three years, with no heroin use on supervised urine testing for 18 months and steady employment. Four weeks ago another doctor started escitalopram 20 mg daily for depression. He has had two days of vomiting and loose stools from a gastrointestinal illness that is now settling.

He has had no syncope, no palpitations and no seizures, and there is no family history of sudden cardiac death. His electrocardiogram today shows sinus rhythm at 52 beats per minute with a measured QT interval of 520 milliseconds. His potassium is 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/L (2.15-2.55) and creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110). His liver function and thyroid function are normal, and he takes no other prescribed or over the counter medication. He tells you that stopping methadone is the one thing he does not want, because the last time his dose was cut he relapsed within a fortnight.

Correct the potassium and magnesium, cease escitalopram and repeat the tracing

subtopic_detail: young woman with patchy scalp hair loss admitting to pulling hairs out when studying under pressure
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19-year-old university student who has noticed thinning over the top and right side of her scalp for the past year. She wears her hair up to disguise it. With some embarrassment she tells you that she pulls hairs out one at a time, mostly in the evenings while studying, and feels a build up of tension beforehand and a sense of relief afterwards.

She says she is not trying to hurt herself and does not want to die. She does not eat the hair. She has always been a worrier but has no low mood, no weight change and sleeps reasonably well. On examination there are ill defined patches of shortened hair of varying lengths over the vertex and right parietal scalp, with no scaling, erythema, scarring or pustules, and the underlying skin looks normal. Eyebrows and eyelashes are intact. Thyroid function, iron studies and a full blood examination arranged by a colleague last month were all within normal limits.

data_table.Distribution: Eyebrows and eyelashes intact, no body hair loss, no nail changes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Commence sertraline titrated to a therapeutic dose and review her response in six weeks
Commence oral olanzapine at a low dose with monitoring of weight and metabolic parameters
Prescribe a potent topical corticosteroid to the affected areas and review her in eight weeks

subtopic_detail: student falling asleep constantly whose knees buckle when he laughs at his friends' jokes
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 20-year-old apprentice electrician who has fallen asleep at his workbench three times in the past month and has been warned by his supervisor. He says he sleeps eight hours a night, wakes unrefreshed, and feels an overwhelming need to sleep by mid morning that he cannot fight off, though a fifteen minute nap leaves him briefly clear headed.

He mentions that for the past year his knees have given way and his jaw has gone slack for a few seconds when he laughs hard with his mates, staying fully aware throughout. He also describes frightening moments on waking where he cannot move for half a minute. He drinks two standard drinks on weekends only, takes no medications, and has a body mass index of 22 kg per square metre with no snoring reported by his partner. His mood is good, he enjoys his sport and his weight is steady. Examination including neurological examination is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg per square metre, normal neurological examination, no goitre, Mallampati class 1 airway

subtopic_detail: woman with severe irritability and despair for the week before each period that lifts once bleeding starts
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old teacher who describes becoming a different person for about a week each month. She becomes intensely irritable, snaps at her partner and her students, feels hopeless and tearful, and sleeps poorly. She has twice taken sick leave because she could not face the classroom.

She says the change lifts within a day or two of her period starting and that she feels completely well for the following fortnight. On your advice she has kept a daily symptom diary through three consecutive cycles, which shows her symptom scores rising sharply about six days before each period, peaking on the two days before bleeding, and returning to baseline by the second day of bleeding, with a clear symptom-free interval each cycle. She is not pregnant and uses condoms. She drinks alcohol rarely, takes no medications, and thyroid function and a full blood examination are within normal limits.

subtopic_detail: treating a colleague who discloses heavy drinking but has taken herself off the roster already
stem:
You are a general practitioner and a 34-year-old surgical registrar has made an appointment with you as a patient. She tells you she has been drinking a bottle of wine most nights for the past eight months since a relationship ended, and scores 22 on the alcohol use disorders identification test.

She tells you she has never operated or attended work while affected by alcohol, and that two weeks ago she recognised the problem, spoke to her director of training, and has been on planned leave since with no patient contact. She has arranged to see an addiction medicine specialist next week and wants your help with the interim management. She is tearful but engaged, denies suicidal ideation, and has no withdrawal symptoms today. Her liver function tests show a gamma glutamyl transferase of 96 U/L (5 to 35) with normal transaminases and bilirubin, and her full blood examination shows a mean cell volume of 99 fL (80 to 98).

subtopic_detail: older woman with failing central vision who sees detailed figures in period costume and knows they are not real
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 82-year-old woman brought in by her daughter, who is worried her mother is developing dementia. For the past three months she has been seeing small figures in old fashioned clothing walking along the skirting board of her lounge room, and sometimes brickwork patterns appearing across the wall.

She describes the images as vivid and detailed, lasting several minutes at a time, usually in the evening. She is quite clear that they are not really there and finds them curious rather than frightening, and she says they never speak to her. She has advanced age related macular degeneration and her corrected visual acuity is 6/60 on the right and counting fingers on the left. She lives alone, manages her own finances and medications, cooks for herself, and scores 29 out of 30 on a standardised cognitive screen. She takes no anticholinergic medications, has no tremor or rigidity, no fluctuating attention and no dream enactment behaviour reported.

subtopic_detail: child who talks freely at home but has not spoken at school in the eight months since starting
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old girl whose teacher has asked her parents to seek help. She has not spoken a single word at school since she started eight months ago, communicating only by pointing and nodding, though she joins in games with two classmates without speaking.

At home she is described as chatty, funny and bossy with her younger brother, and she speaks freely to her parents and grandparents. She spoke to you briefly in the waiting room while playing with her mother but has not spoken since you entered the room. Her parents report that she reached all her speech milestones on time and that her vocabulary and sentence structure are age appropriate at home. She makes eye contact with you, follows your pointing, brings a drawing to show her mother and looks to her for a reaction. There are no repetitive behaviours or restricted interests, her hearing was tested and normal last year, and there are no concerns about her learning.

subtopic_detail: man with an evening urge to move his legs relieved by walking and a low ferritin on screening
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old man who cannot get to sleep. For the past year he has had a deeply unpleasant crawling sensation in both calves that builds during the evening while he sits watching television and forces him to get up and walk around. Walking relieves it completely within a minute, and it returns once he sits down again.

He is worst between about 9 pm and 1 am and says he is fine during the working day. His wife says his legs do not kick once he is asleep. He has no back pain, no radiation down the leg, and no numbness or weakness. He takes no antihistamines, antidepressants or antipsychotics and drinks two cups of coffee before midday only. On examination pedal pulses are present and symmetrical, ankle reflexes are intact, and sensation and power are normal in both legs. His ferritin is 38 mcg/L (30 to 300), haemoglobin is 142 g/L (130 to 180) and transferrin saturation is 16 per cent (16 to 45).

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical present pedal pulses, intact ankle reflexes, normal power and sensation in both lower limbs

subtopic_detail: older woman certain that mites live in her skin who brings in skin flakes sealed in a container
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 71-year-old woman for the fifth time in three months about insects living under her skin. She has been treated twice with topical permethrin and once with oral ivermectin by a colleague and once by a dermatologist, with no change. She has fumigated her flat twice and has thrown out her mattress.

She places a small plastic container on your desk containing skin flakes, lint and a hair, and asks you to send it to the laboratory to prove the infestation. She is entirely certain about it, says the sensation of movement is constant, and will not consider any other explanation, though she holds no other unusual beliefs and there is no persecutory theme. She lives alone, manages her finances, and scores 28 out of 30 on a standardised cognitive screen. On examination there are linear excoriations and crusted erosions on the forearms and upper back, all within reach, with no burrows in the finger webs and no rash on the trunk. Full blood examination, renal function, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and a urine drug screen are all within normal limits.

subtopic_detail: man eighteen months after his wife died who sets her place at the table and cannot accept she is gone
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 67-year-old man eighteen months after his wife of forty years died of pancreatic cancer. His daughter has encouraged him to come. He tells you he still sets her place at the dinner table each evening, has not moved any of her belongings, and spends several hours most days listening to voicemail messages she left him.

He says he cannot accept that she is gone, feels that part of himself died with her, and avoids the shopping centre they used to visit because it is unbearable. He has withdrawn from the bowls club he attended for twenty years. He describes intense yearning every day rather than waves that come and go, and says life has no purpose without her. He does not feel worthless, his appetite and concentration are reasonable, and he still enjoys his grandson's visits. He denies thoughts of ending his life but says he would not mind if he did not wake up. He drinks two beers most evenings, the same as before she died, and takes no medications.

data_table.Mental state: Tearful when speaking of his wife, affect reactive to other topics, no psychomotor retardation, no guilt or worthlessness

data_table.Function: Withdrawn from bowls club and social contacts, maintains self care, shopping and finances

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange admission to an older persons mental health unit for assessment of his suicide risk
Commence an antidepressant at a therapeutic dose and review his response after six weeks
Reassure him that this is a normal response to losing a spouse and review him in three months
Refer him to a community bereavement support group and encourage a return to his bowls club
Refer for a structured grief focused psychotherapy specifically targeting the loss

subtopic_detail: older man with abrupt memory complaints who answers most cognitive questions by saying he does not know
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 74-year-old retired accountant brought in by his son, who is worried about dementia. The son says his father's memory problems began quite suddenly about four months ago, within weeks of the death of a close friend, and have been at much the same level since.

The patient himself is the one complaining, telling you repeatedly and with distress that his mind has gone and that he is a burden. During cognitive testing he answers I do not know to most questions with little apparent effort, but when you encourage him and give extra time he recalls two of three words and correctly names the prime minister. His son reports he has stopped going to the golf club, wakes at 4 am, has lost 5 kg and has stopped reading the newspaper he read daily for fifty years. He has never got lost driving, manages his own medications correctly, and has had no falls, hallucinations or tremor. Thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, renal function, calcium and a full blood examination are within normal limits.

subtopic_detail: man weeping uncontrollably at trivial remarks after a stroke who denies feeling sad while it happens
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 68-year-old man ten weeks after a left middle cerebral artery infarct. His wife raises that he bursts into uncontrollable sobbing several times a day, often triggered by something trivial such as a television advertisement or being greeted at the door.

The episodes last a minute or two, stop as abruptly as they begin, and he is mortified by them. He tells you clearly that he does not feel sad while it is happening and that the crying seems to come from nowhere and bears no relation to how he feels. Between episodes he says his mood is reasonable, he looks forward to his grandchildren visiting, he is engaging well with rehabilitation and is pleased with his walking progress. He sleeps well, his appetite is good and his weight is stable. He has a residual mild right arm weakness and mild expressive dysphasia. He denies any suicidal thoughts, and a cognitive screen is unremarkable for his dysphasia.

subtopic_detail: man in his late fifties with new disinhibition and loss of empathy referred as late onset bipolar disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 58-year-old builder referred by his general practitioner with a question of late onset bipolar disorder. Over the past two years his wife has watched him change from a considerate man into someone who makes crude remarks to strangers, laughed when their neighbour described her husband's cancer diagnosis, and was formally warned at work for walking off a job site mid shift.

He now eats several packets of biscuits daily, has gained 12 kg, and insists on the same lunch at the same cafe at the same time each day and becomes agitated if this is disrupted. His wife says he is not elated, does not need less sleep and talks no faster than usual. He is unbothered by any of it and says his wife worries too much. His father developed a similar change at 60 and died in a nursing home at 66. On testing he scores 27 out of 30 on a standardised cognitive screen with intact orientation and recall, but he names only five animals in a minute and continues an incorrect response pattern after being corrected.

stem:

Three weeks ago you started her on sertraline for a depressive episode and she had begun to sleep and eat a little better. Over the past four days she has become vague and muddled, has been unsteady on her feet with two near falls, and vomited twice yesterday.

She has hypertension treated with indapamide, which she has taken for six years, and no other medical history. She has not had diarrhoea, fever, cough or dysuria, and there has been no change to her fluid intake. On examination she is drowsy but rousable and oriented to person only, with moist mucous membranes, no postural drop in blood pressure, jugular venous pressure not elevated and no peripheral oedema. Chest is clear and the abdomen is soft. lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange overnight home oximetry and review the tracing in the clinic
Trial of a third antidepressant from a different pharmacological class
Measure thyroid function with iron studies and vitamin B12 levels
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast within a month
Refer for polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test

subtopic_detail: recognising drug induced inner restlessness that has been misread as worsening agitation
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to the ward about a 46-year-old man with schizophrenia whose antipsychotic was changed to aripiprazole three weeks ago. The nursing staff have documented increasing agitation and have given two doses of an oral as needed antipsychotic over the past two days, after each of which they record that he became more unsettled rather than less.

He tells you that he cannot describe it properly but that he feels a dreadful restlessness inside, that he cannot stay in a chair and has to keep moving, and that it is there from the moment he wakes until he falls asleep. He paces the corridor and rocks from foot to foot while standing talking to you. He says his psychotic symptoms have actually improved and denies feeling frightened or angry with anyone.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
