data_table.Examination: Constant shifting of weight while standing, inability to remain seated for more than a minute, no tremor, no cogwheel rigidity, no orofacial dyskinesia, mental state examination shows settled thought content with improved delusional conviction
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 140 micrograms/L (30 to 300), full blood count within normal limits, creatine kinase within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reduce the antipsychotic dose and commence propranolol for the symptom
Increase the antipsychotic dose to settle what appears to be agitation
Commence benzatropine and review the response over the next few days
Commence a dopamine agonist taken in the evening before he goes to bed
Commence oral iron replacement and recheck the ferritin in three months

subtopic_detail: acting on a markedly prolonged QT interval with correctable electrolyte abnormalities and additive drug effects
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on an inpatient unit reviewing a 52-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder. She has been taking citalopram 40 mg daily and haloperidol, and over the past week she has had repeated vomiting attributed to a gastrointestinal illness and has eaten very little.

This morning she felt light headed on standing and the nursing staff obtained an electrocardiogram. She has no chest pain and no palpitations, has never had a syncopal episode, and has no known cardiac disease. A previous electrocardiogram taken on admission six weeks ago was reported as normal. Her results are available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 58, blood pressure 106/68, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, no murmur, heart sounds dual, chest clear, no peripheral oedema, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.75 to 1.05), corrected calcium within normal limits, creatinine mildly raised, thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus bradycardia at 58 beats per minute with a corrected QT interval of 510 milliseconds, no ischaemic changes, compared with 430 milliseconds six weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue both medications and repeat the electrocardiogram in a week
Replace potassium and magnesium with continuous cardiac monitoring
Cease the antipsychotic alone and continue the antidepressant unchanged
Give intravenous magnesium only if torsades de pointes actually occurs
Switch immediately to a different antipsychotic at an equivalent dose

subtopic_detail: involuntary movements and a suggestive family history in apparent treatment resistant depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 41-year-old man referred with eighteen months of low mood, irritability and loss of interest that has not responded to adequate trials of two antidepressants. He works as an accountant and has been placed on a performance review at work.

His wife says the bigger change is that he has become blunt to the point of rudeness with her family, has spent several thousand dollars on impulse purchases, and no longer initiates anything at home. She also mentions that he fidgets constantly, drops cups and cutlery, and that his walking has become unsteady in a way he does not seem to notice. He has never been prescribed an antipsychotic or any dopamine blocking medication. His mother died at 55 in a psychiatric hospital with what the family were told was early dementia.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Brief irregular involuntary movements of the fingers and face incorporated into voluntary gestures, motor impersistence with inability to maintain tongue protrusion for ten seconds, slowed initiation of horizontal saccades, wide based unsteady gait, no cogwheel rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function within normal limits, vitamin B12 within normal limits, syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology negative, full blood count within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial a third antidepressant from a different class for three months
Send the huntingtin gene test from the clinic today and phone the result
Refer to a neurogenetics service for counselling before any genetic test
Commence an antipsychotic to suppress the involuntary movements now
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and review the report

subtopic_detail: weighing a contested medication association against active suicidal ideation in an adolescent
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 17-year-old boy who is eight weeks into a course of isotretinoin prescribed by a dermatologist for severe nodulocystic acne that had scarred his cheeks and back.

His mother booked the appointment because he has stopped going to soccer training, spends most of his time in his room and has become monosyllabic at home. Seen alone, he tells you his mood has been flat for about five weeks, that he has stopped enjoying things he used to, and that he sleeps poorly. When you ask directly, he says that in the past fortnight he has sometimes thought that everyone would be better off without him, though he has no plan and has never harmed himself. He had a depressive episode at 15 that responded to psychological therapy alone.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Flattened affect with reduced spontaneous speech, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, passive thoughts that others would be better off without him without plan or intent, marked improvement in the acne itself
data_table.Investigations: Liver function within normal limits, fasting lipids within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Halve the isotretinoin dose and review the mood in two weeks' time
Continue the isotretinoin and start an antidepressant at the same visit
Continue the isotretinoin and review him in the clinic in four weeks
Cease the isotretinoin and arrange an urgent mental health assessment
Reassure that the association is unproven and continue the treatment

subtopic_detail: pursuing copper studies when caeruloplasmin sits within the reference range in a young person with psychiatric and movement signs
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 23-year-old man admitted under your team. Over ten months he has become increasingly irritable and disinhibited, has failed two university semesters after previously doing well, and four months ago was diagnosed with a first episode of psychosis at another hospital.

Risperidone was started at 1 mg daily and within a week he developed marked rigidity and a coarse tremor, which his previous team described as an unusually severe reaction to a low dose. His speech has become slurred over the past two months and his handwriting has shrunk and become untidy. His mother has noticed he drools on his pillow. He drinks alcohol rarely and his urine drug screen is negative. He has one older sister who is well.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Dysarthria with hypophonia, coarse proximal tremor of both arms on posture, cogwheel rigidity at both wrists, micrographia, drooling, no asterixis, no jaundice, liver edge not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 78 U/L (less than 35), bilirubin within normal limits, international normalised ratio within normal limits, serum caeruloplasmin 0.21 g/L (0.20 to 0.60), haemoglobin within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat the serum caeruloplasmin level in three months and reassess
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with susceptibility sequences
Measure the total serum copper concentration on a fasting sample
Percutaneous liver biopsy for quantitative hepatic copper content
Collect a 24 hour urine sample for quantitative copper excretion

subtopic_detail: choosing between behavioural therapy and dopamine blockade as the first treatment for tics that have become socially impairing
stem:
You are the registrar in a general paediatric and adolescent clinic seeing an 11-year-old boy brought by his mother. Since he was seven he has had bouts of blinking, shoulder shrugging and head jerking, and for the past two years he has also made a repeated throat clearing noise. The movements wax and wane, shift between body parts and disappear when he is absorbed in building models.

His mother says two boys in his class have started imitating the noise and he now asks to eat lunch in the library. He is in the top group for reading, sleeps well and has no rituals, counting or checking. He is not distractible in class and his teacher reports no difficulty with sustained attention. He can hold the movements back for a few minutes but describes a build up of tension in his neck that only settles once he lets them out.

data_table.Examination: Intermittent eye blinking and right shoulder shrug during the consultation, throat clearing three times, neurological examination otherwise normal
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Reassurance alone with a planned clinic review in twelve months
Referral for comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics
Low dose risperidone titrated slowly over the next four weeks
Clonidine at night with blood pressure checked at each review
Aripiprazole commenced at low dose with metabolic monitoring

subtopic_detail: managing amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea appearing on a stable antipsychotic dose when the prolactin sits in the drug induced rather than tumour range
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24-year-old woman in the community clinic. She has taken risperidone 4 mg daily for eight months after a first episode of psychosis and has been well, working part time and attending university.

Today she tells you her periods stopped four months ago and that she has noticed milk leaking from both breasts when she showers. A urine pregnancy test in clinic is negative. She has no headache, no change in her vision and no galactorrhoea before starting treatment. She takes no other medication and does not use cannabis or other substances. She is clear that she wants to stay on treatment because the psychosis frightened her.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral expressible milky discharge, visual fields full to confrontation, no acromegalic features
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1680 mIU/L (100 to 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa
Cross titrate from risperidone to aripiprazole over three weeks
Add cabergoline weekly and continue the current risperidone dose
Start a combined oral contraceptive pill to restore her periods
Cease antipsychotic treatment and monitor for symptom recurrence

subtopic_detail: interpreting dilute high volume urine with a rising sodium in a long term lithium patient whose glucose is normal
stem:
You are the registrar in a community mental health service reviewing a 46-year-old woman who has taken lithium for bipolar affective disorder for eight years with no admissions in that time. She tells you she is passing very large amounts of pale urine and is getting up three or four times most nights, and that she carries a two litre bottle everywhere because her mouth feels dry.

A measured collection shows a urine volume of 4.6 L over twenty four hours. She has not changed her dose and takes no diuretic, no antipsychotic and no other regular medication. After she was kept without fluids under supervision for six hours the urine remained dilute and her serum sodium rose further.

data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, no postural drop, no goitre, weight stable
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 148 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45 to 90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 62 mL/min/1.73m2, random glucose 5.2 mmol/L (3.0 to 7.7), serum lithium 0.71 mmol/L (0.6 to 0.8), urine osmolality 178 mOsm/kg (300 to 900)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence amiloride and review the ongoing indication for lithium
Commence desmopressin nasal spray and recheck the sodium weekly
Restrict her fluid intake to 1.5 L daily and repeat the electrolytes
Arrange an oral glucose tolerance test before altering any treatment
Cease lithium abruptly today and substitute sodium valproate instead

subtopic_detail: first line treatment for compulsive sports betting presenting behind a complaint of insomnia and low mood
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 38-year-old carpenter who has booked a long appointment for three months of poor sleep and feeling flat. He falls asleep easily but wakes at two in the morning and cannot settle again.

When you ask what is on his mind at that hour he becomes tearful and describes betting on sport through an app on his phone. He has lost about forty thousand dollars over two years, has taken out a personal loan his partner does not know about, and has been putting larger amounts on to win back what he lost. He drinks two standard drinks on a Friday and uses no other substances. He denies any thoughts of ending his life and says he has tried three times to delete the app.

data_table.Examination: Appears tired and tearful, no psychomotor retardation, normal cognition
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy directed at his gambling
Start sertraline and review his mood symptoms in four weeks
Prescribe naltrexone daily and arrange liver function monitoring
Arrange financial counselling as the sole intervention for now
Advise self exclusion from betting platforms and review in three months

subtopic_detail: a child who talks freely at home but has never spoken at school, with normal language milestones and a normal hearing screen
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a community clinic seeing a 6-year-old girl referred by her school. In the fourteen months since she started school she has not spoken a word to her teacher or to any classmate, although she will nod, point and hand over written notes.

Her parents bring a phone recording in which she is chatting and singing at length with her younger brother at home. Her milestones were normal, she joined words into sentences before two, and a formal hearing assessment last term was normal. She makes eye contact with you, brings a toy over to show you and plays reciprocally with her mother in the room. There are no repetitive behaviours and no restricted interests. She flushes and freezes when you ask her a direct question.

data_table.Examination: Mute with the examiner but socially engaged non verbally, cranial nerves and oromotor examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Pure tone audiometry within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for graded exposure behavioural therapy delivered with the school
Refer to speech pathology for assessment of expressive language delay
Refer for a diagnostic assessment for autism spectrum disorder instead
Commence fluoxetine at low dose and review her progress in six weeks
Advise the school to wait a further six months for her to settle in

subtopic_detail: a young man seeking rhinoplasty for a defect others cannot see, with three hours daily of mirror checking
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 22-year-old apprentice electrician who asks for a referral to a plastic surgeon. He believes the bridge of his nose is twisted and that people stare at it.

He spends about three hours a day checking his profile in mirrors and in the reflective glass of shop windows, takes photographs from different angles to compare, and has stopped going to his football club social nights. He has cancelled two family gatherings in the past month. He has no concerns about his weight, eats normally and his body mass index is 23 kg/m2. He accepts that his family and friends tell him his nose looks ordinary but says he cannot make himself believe it. On examination his nose is symmetrical with no deviation.

data_table.Examination: Nasal bridge straight and symmetrical, no septal deviation, no excoriation of the skin
data_table.Investigations: None indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer to a plastic surgeon for an opinion on corrective rhinoplasty
Commence olanzapine at low dose for a fixed belief about his body
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy adapted to appearance concerns
Reassure him about his appearance and review again in three months
Start fluoxetine and arrange psychological review only if it fails

subtopic_detail: sleepiness on night duty with an inability to sleep during the day in a rotating roster worker whose sleep is normal on leave
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old intensive care nurse who has worked a rotating roster with blocks of four night shifts for the past eight months. She asks for something to help her sleep.

She describes lying awake until midday after a night shift, managing only three to four broken hours, and then fighting to stay awake from about three in the morning on the next shift. She has twice caught herself drifting at the wheel on the drive home. On her two week annual leave in April she slept seven to eight hours a night without difficulty and felt well. She does not snore, has no witnessed pauses in breathing, and her body mass index is 22 kg/m2. Her partner sleeps in the same room and reports no kicking or restless movements.

data_table.Examination: Mallampati class 1, neck circumference 32 cm, no goitre, mood and cognition normal
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies including ferritin and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Prescribe zopiclone to be taken before each daytime sleep period
Refer for overnight polysomnography before any treatment is started
Prescribe modafinil each night shift and arrange follow up in a month
Plan timed bright light, protected daytime sleep and a pre shift nap
Commence melatonin at bedtime and review her sleep diary in six weeks

subtopic_detail: persistent detachment and a flat unreal quality to the world after a single cannabis episode, with reality testing preserved
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 20-year-old university student referred by his general practitioner. Eight months ago, at a party, he smoked a much stronger cannabis preparation than he was used to and felt intensely frightened for several hours.

Since that night he has felt, in his words, like he is watching himself from just behind his own shoulder, and says his hands sometimes look as though they belong to someone else. Colours seem washed out and the street where he grew up looks like a stage set. He finds all of this distressing and says he knows perfectly well that it is his own mind playing tricks and that the world has not really changed. He has not used cannabis or any other substance since that night. He has no gaps in his memory for events or for personal information, hears no voices and holds no unusual beliefs.

data_table.Examination: Cooperative, reactive affect, speech normal in rate and form, no thought disorder, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Cannabis induced psychotic disorder with residual perceptual features
Persistent depersonalisation and derealisation disorder after cannabis
Panic disorder presenting with prominent dissociative experiences
Schizophrenia presenting with predominantly negative and odd symptoms
Post-traumatic stress disorder of the dissociative subtype after a scare

subtopic_detail: a severely neglected preschooler in foster care whose social reciprocity is improving with placement rather than remaining fixed
stem:
You are the registrar in a child development clinic seeing a 4-year-old boy placed with a foster carer eighteen months ago. Before the placement he lived in conditions of severe neglect with several changes of caregiver.

The referral says he seldom goes to an adult for comfort when he falls and rarely responds when his carer tries to soothe him, and that he shows little positive emotion during play. His carer adds that in the past six months he has begun to bring her drawings unprompted, glances back at her when something surprises him, and has started feeding a toy dinosaur with a plastic spoon. His vocabulary and sentence structure are appropriate for his age and he understands two step instructions. He lines his cars up occasionally but plays with them as cars as well, and he has no repetitive mannerisms and no sensory aversions.

data_table.Examination: Subdued affect, limited comfort seeking, emerging shared attention with the carer, growth on the fiftieth centile
data_table.Investigations: Hearing and vision screening both within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Autism spectrum disorder with an associated language strength profile
Global developmental delay arising from prolonged early understimulation
Disinhibited social engagement disorder following the early deprivation
Childhood depressive disorder with marked anhedonia and social withdrawal
Reactive attachment disorder arising from grossly insufficient early care

subtopic_detail: yearning and preoccupation sixteen months after a spousal death that has not moved despite an adequate antidepressant trial
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 58-year-old woman whose husband died sixteen months ago after a short illness. She was started on sertraline by a colleague six months ago and has taken 100 mg daily for the past four months without missing doses.

She describes an ache of longing for him that fills most of the day, spends hours going through his photographs and messages, and has not been able to open the door of his study. She says she still cannot take in that he is gone. She lights up describing her granddaughter's swimming carnival last weekend and went to it willingly. She eats normally, her weight is unchanged, she feels she was a good wife and she has no thoughts of harming herself. There is no psychomotor slowing and she is not self critical.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when speaking of her husband, warm and reactive otherwise, no psychomotor retardation, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, thyroid stimulating hormone and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer for a structured psychological therapy targeting her grief
Increase the sertraline to 150 mg daily and review her again in six weeks
Add low dose quetiapine at night to settle her ruminative preoccupation
Reassure her that this is normal bereavement and review in six months
Refer her to a community bereavement support group as the only measure

subtopic_detail: the hypnotic itself as the cause of a fall in an older woman, and how to stop it without simply substituting another sedative
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 78-year-old woman two weeks after she fell getting up to the toilet at three in the morning and fractured her left wrist. She has taken zopiclone 7.5 mg nightly for the past four years, started after her husband died.

She says the tablet no longer works as it once did and that she often feels foggy for an hour or two after waking. She lives alone in a single storey home, uses no walking aid, and her postural blood pressure, visual acuity and gait speed have all been checked and were normal. Her vitamin D and calcium are adequate and she is on a bisphosphonate. She has no other sedating medication, drinks no alcohol, and her cognitive screening score is normal. She is frightened of both falling again and of lying awake all night.

data_table.Examination: Left wrist in a cast, timed up and go test 10 seconds, no postural drop, Mini Mental State Examination 29 of 30
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, thyroid stimulating hormone and corrected calcium all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her insomnia?

options.text: Substitute temazepam 10 mg at night as a safer hypnotic alternative
Cease the zopiclone tonight and advise that any rebound will settle
Taper the zopiclone gradually alongside cognitive behavioural therapy
Add prolonged release melatonin and continue her usual zopiclone dose
Continue the zopiclone given her normal gait and vision assessments

subtopic_detail: new self directed hitting and food refusal in a non speaking adult with intellectual disability whose environment has not changed
stem:
You are the registrar in a community disability health service asked to see a 34-year-old man with severe intellectual disability who does not use speech. Over the past three weeks he has begun hitting the side of his own head with an open hand, mostly in the evenings, and has become resistant at mealtimes.

His support workers report that his house, staff roster, day program and routine are all unchanged, and that no new medication has been started. He is still drinking his usual fluids and will accept yoghurt and soup, but pushes away the toast and apple he previously ate every day. He has lost 2 kg in three weeks. He is afebrile and his bowels are opening daily. The behaviour support practitioner has asked you to prescribe something to settle him before a functional assessment can be scheduled.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, blood pressure 126/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Resists approach to the face, no external swelling, chest and abdomen unremarkable, no guarding
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, C reactive protein and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence risperidone at low dose and review the behaviour in two weeks
Refer for a functional behaviour assessment and await its recommendations
Commence sertraline for a presumed underlying depressive presentation
Undertake a systematic physical examination including the mouth and ears
Start regular paracetamol and reassess the behaviour after one week

subtopic_detail: recurrent winter depressive episodes with oversleeping and carbohydrate craving that remit each spring in a high latitude Australian city
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old woman in Hobart in mid July. For the third consecutive year she has become flat, unmotivated and tearful from about May onward.

She sleeps ten to eleven hours and still wakes unrefreshed, craves bread and sweet food, and has gained 5 kg since April. She finds it hardest in the first hours of the day. Each of the two previous episodes lifted completely in September without treatment and she was fully well through summer, working and socialising normally. She has never had a period of elevated mood, reduced need for sleep or overspending. Her thyroid function, ferritin and vitamin D have been checked this month and are normal, and she has no thoughts of self-harm.

data_table.Examination: Slowed but reactive, no psychomotor retardation on formal testing, weight 74 kg
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone, ferritin, vitamin D and full blood count all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first treatment?

options.text: Commence fluoxetine 20 mg each morning and review her again in four weeks
Prescribe high dose colecalciferol weekly and reassess her mood in a month
Arrange bright light therapy for thirty minutes soon after waking each day
Start agomelatine at night with liver function testing before and during
Begin lithium augmentation given the recurrent and periodic course she has

subtopic_detail: choosing between magnetic stimulation and electroconvulsive therapy after two failed antidepressant trials in a patient who is eating and not suicidal
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 45-year-old plumber with a current major depressive episode of fourteen months. He completed twelve weeks of escitalopram 20 mg daily and then ten weeks of venlafaxine 225 mg daily, both taken as prescribed, with no meaningful change.

He has also had sixteen sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy. He is eating and drinking normally, has lost no weight, and continues to work three days a week although he says he is going through the motions. He denies any intent to end his life and has made no plans. He holds no delusional beliefs about guilt, illness or poverty, and there is no stupor, mutism or waxy flexibility. He has never had a seizure and takes no other medication.

data_table.Examination: Reduced spontaneous speech, reactive affect, no psychomotor retardation, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next treatment?

options.text: Switch to a third antidepressant from a different pharmacological class
Arrange an urgent course of electroconvulsive therapy under anaesthesia
Refer for a course of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation
Augment the venlafaxine with lithium and monitor levels and renal function
Commence a course of intravenous ketamine infusions in a day unit setting

subtopic_detail: repugnant intrusive images of harming a newborn with preserved insight and checking behaviour, seven weeks after birth
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29-year-old woman at her baby's seven week check. She asks to speak to you alone and then, with great difficulty, tells you that pictures keep coming into her mind of the baby slipping from her arms on the stairs and of a knife.

She describes the images as horrible and says they make her feel sick. She has started carrying the baby only on the ground floor, has moved the kitchen knives to a high cupboard, and checks the baby's breathing eight or nine times a night. She says she would never do any of it and that she cannot understand why her mind produces it. She is sleeping when the baby sleeps, is feeding the baby well and is delighted by him when he smiles. She is fully oriented, hears nothing others cannot hear, and holds no beliefs that the baby is abnormal or in danger from others.

data_table.Examination: Anxious and ashamed, fully oriented, no perceptual abnormality, warm and attuned interaction with the infant
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone, full blood count and ferritin all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent admission to a mother and baby unit for further observation
Notify child protection services and arrange supervised contact meanwhile
Commence olanzapine at night and review her in the surgery within a week
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention
Reassure her that these thoughts are common and review her in six weeks

subtopic_detail: a primigravida with panic level dread of giving birth requesting an elective caesarean at twenty four weeks
stem:
You are the general practitioner providing shared antenatal care for a 32-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 24 weeks. She asks you to write to the hospital requesting a caesarean section.

When you ask what worries her she becomes breathless and tearful, and describes lying awake imagining tearing and bleeding. She has left two antenatal classes early, cannot watch a birth scene on television, and has been avoiding her sister who is also pregnant. This fear has been present since her teens and long predates this pregnancy. She has had no previous births and no gynaecological surgery or assault. The pregnancy itself is progressing normally with a cephalic presentation, normal growth and no medical complications. She has a supportive partner and is otherwise functioning well at work.

data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height appropriate for dates, blood pressure 112/68, distressed when discussing labour
data_table.Investigations: Routine antenatal screening including morphology scan all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Write supporting an elective caesarean section to be booked at 39 weeks
Commence sertraline now and review her symptoms again in four weeks
Reassure her that most first births are uncomplicated and review at 28 weeks
Refer to the obstetric anaesthetist to plan early epidural analgesia in labour
Refer to perinatal mental health for therapy directed at her fear of birth

subtopic_detail: documented heavy prenatal alcohol exposure with impairment across several neurodevelopmental domains but no facial features
stem:
You are the registrar in a child development clinic seeing a 7-year-old boy who has lived with his grandmother since he was two. Child protection records that his mother drank heavily throughout the pregnancy are available and his grandmother confirms them.

His teacher describes him as unable to stay on task, out of his seat, and two years behind in numeracy despite intensive support. His grandmother says he will walk off with anyone who speaks kindly to him, cannot be trusted near the road, and cannot manage a morning routine even with a picture chart. He is warm, makes good eye contact and has age-appropriate conversational language. His face is unremarkable, with normal philtrum, upper lip and palpebral fissures. His head circumference is on the second centile and his height and weight are on the twenty fifth.

data_table.Examination: Head circumference second centile, no dysmorphic facial features, neurological examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Hearing and vision screening normal, chromosomal microarray previously reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence a trial of methylphenidate for his inattention and overactivity
Refer for a diagnostic assessment for autism spectrum disorder in the first instance
Repeat the chromosomal microarray and add fragile X testing before proceeding
Arrange school based behaviour support and review his progress in six months
Refer for a multidisciplinary neurodevelopmental assessment across all domains

subtopic_detail: a second relapse that followed stopping oral medication, and whether that history makes the illness treatment resistant
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar planning discharge for a 26-year-old man admitted three weeks ago with persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations. This is his second admission in eighteen months.

On both occasions his housemate and his sister describe him as stopping his aripiprazole tablets several weeks before becoming unwell again, and on both occasions symptoms resolved within two to three weeks of restarting the same drug at the same dose. He is now free of hallucinations and no longer holds the persecutory belief. He says tablets remind him every morning that he is ill, and that he wants above all not to come back into hospital. He uses no substances and a urine drug screen on admission was negative. He has had no extrapyramidal symptoms and his weight and metabolic screen are unchanged.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no perceptual abnormality, no thought disorder, no abnormal movements
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, liver function tests, fasting lipids and glucose all within normal limits

lead_in: What is most likely to reduce his risk of a further relapse?

options.text: Increase the oral aripiprazole dose and continue it at the higher dose
Transition to a long-acting injectable antipsychotic before he is discharged
Commence clozapine with the required haematological monitoring program
Arrange a weekly dose administration aid with pharmacy supervised dosing
Continue oral treatment and reserve an injectable agent for any third relapse

subtopic_detail: lifelong inattention in a woman referred with anxiety whose symptoms have not moved on an adequate antidepressant trial
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 27-year-old graphic designer who was started on sertraline six months ago for anxiety and has taken 100 mg daily for the last four months. She says she feels no different.

She describes her worry as being almost entirely about work: unopened emails, three projects started and none finished, and a recent formal warning for a missed deadline. She loses her keys and wallet most weeks and has been late to every appointment she has made with you. Her mother has kept her old school reports, which from age eight describe a bright girl who drifts off, does not finish her work and needs constant redirection. She sleeps well, her mood is reactive and she has never had a panic attack or a period of avoidance of social situations. She drinks alcohol rarely and uses no other substances.

data_table.Examination: Engaged and articulate, tangential at times, no psychomotor change, cognition grossly intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, ferritin, thyroid stimulating hormone and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the sertraline to 150 mg daily and review her symptoms in six weeks
Diagnose generalised anxiety disorder and refer for cognitive behavioural therapy
Commence a trial of methylphenidate and assess her response over four weeks
Refer for an autism spectrum diagnostic assessment given her social difficulties
Gather the childhood school reports and refer for a structured ADHD assessment

subtopic_detail: an abrupt severe occipital headache with extreme hypertension two hours after aged cheese and cured meat in a patient on an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 52-year-old man brought in by his wife from a wedding reception two hours ago. He has taken tranylcypromine for eighteen months for a depressive illness that failed several other treatments.

He developed a sudden pounding headache at the back of his head, followed by a thumping heartbeat, drenching sweat and neck stiffness that he describes as muscles rather than pain on flexion. His wife says he ate a grazing platter of aged cheddar, salami and prosciutto because he had forgotten which foods he was meant to avoid. He is fully alert with no focal neurological signs and no photophobia. A non contrast computed tomography scan of his brain performed on arrival shows no haemorrhage. He takes no other regular medication and used no recreational drugs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, blood pressure 215/125, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented, pupils equal and reactive, no focal deficit, fundi show no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia without ischaemic change, troponin and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous phentolamine titrated against the blood pressure response
Intravenous metoprolol given in small increments until the pulse settles
Sublingual nifedipine repeated once if the pressure remains above target
Oral captopril with hourly blood pressure monitoring in the resuscitation bay
Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia before any antihypertensive is started

subtopic_detail: advising parents about episodes of screaming early in the night that the child cannot recall next morning
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing the parents of a 4-year-old boy who have come without him because they are frightened by what happens at night.

They describe that about ninety minutes after he falls asleep he sits up and screams, his eyes are open but he does not seem to see them, he is sweaty with a racing heart, and he pushes them away when they try to comfort him. It lasts around five minutes and then he lies down and sleeps. In the morning he is cheerful and has no memory of it at all. It happens two or three times a week and always in the first part of the night. He started four-year-old kindergarten six weeks ago and has been going to bed later than usual. He is developing normally, has no daytime symptoms and there is no snoring.

data_table.Examination: Well grown and developmentally appropriate on parental report, no dysmorphic features described, tonsils not enlarged on a recent review, no daytime behavioural concerns reported by kindergarten
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a low dose benzodiazepine at night for the next three months
Refer for overnight polysomnography to characterise the nocturnal episodes
Advise the parents to wake him fully during each episode and comfort him
Start an antidepressant to reduce the anxiety underlying the night time distress
Reassure the parents, advise on safety, and address his sleep schedule

subtopic_detail: responding to escalating prescribed opioid use for chronic non cancer pain with declining function
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 47-year-old man who has taken sustained release oxycodone for chronic low back pain for five years. He has inherited this prescription from a previous doctor and asks you today for an increase.

He is now on 80 mg of oral morphine equivalent daily, having started on 20 mg. He tells you the pain is no better than when he started and that he has stopped playing golf and has been off work for two years. He says he gets a few hours of relief after each dose and is watching the clock towards the end of the interval. He has run out early twice in the past four months. He drinks no alcohol and uses no illicit drugs, and a urine drug screen shows only his prescribed medication. He has not had a trial of any non-pharmacological pain program. His imaging shows degenerative change only.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No focal neurological deficit in either leg, straight leg raise negative bilaterally, reflexes symmetrical, no saddle anaesthesia, no bladder or bowel disturbance, guarded lumbar movement
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for the prescribed opioid only, lumbar magnetic resonance imaging shows degenerative disc disease with no nerve root compression, liver and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the dose as requested and review his pain scores in four weeks
Cease the opioid abruptly today and manage any withdrawal symptomatically
Negotiate a structured tapering plan with a broader pain management approach
Add a benzodiazepine to help with the muscle spasm and his difficulty sleeping
Discharge him from the practice and advise him to find another prescriber

subtopic_detail: responding to a markedly prolonged corrected QT interval in an older patient whose antidepressant dose exceeds the age adjusted maximum
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to review a 71-year-old woman admitted with a fractured wrist after a fall at home. She has taken citalopram 40 mg daily for two years for recurrent major depression and her mood has been stable.

The orthopaedic team have sent an electrocardiogram because she described two episodes of feeling faint in the week before the fall. She takes no other regular medication apart from a thiazide diuretic for hypertension and a proton pump inhibitor. She has had no chest pain and no palpitations. Her potassium is 3.1 mmol/L and her magnesium is 0.62 mmol/L. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 64 beats per minute with a corrected QT interval of 512 ms, and a tracing from three years ago showed a corrected QT interval of 430 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 64/min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented, mood euthymic with reactive affect, no psychotic features, no tremor or clonus, heart sounds dual with no murmur, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Corrected QT interval 512 ms against 430 ms three years ago, potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.30 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue citalopram at 40 mg and repeat the electrocardiogram in three months
Switch to amitriptyline at a low dose, which also treats her neuropathic pain
Stop all antidepressant treatment permanently and monitor her mood in clinic
Halve the citalopram to 20 mg and take no other action on the abnormal results
Correct the electrolytes, cease citalopram and change to a safer antidepressant

subtopic_detail: recognising sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter in a young man referred with suspected depression
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19-year-old university student referred by his mother because he sleeps all the time and she is worried he is depressed.

He describes falling asleep in lectures and once while sitting on a bus, and says brief naps leave him refreshed for an hour or two. He is not sad, is looking forward to the summer, has been going out with friends and has not lost interest in his hobbies. His appetite and weight are unchanged and he denies any thoughts of self-harm. He mentions that when his friends make him laugh hard his knees buckle and his jaw goes slack for a few seconds while he stays fully aware, and that he sometimes wakes unable to move for half a minute and sees a figure in the doorway that is not there.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, normal power and reflexes, no ptosis, no fatigable weakness, body mass index 24 kg/m2, mood euthymic with reactive affect
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, thyroid function and fasting glucose all within normal limits, Epworth Sleepiness Scale score 19 out of 24

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Major depressive disorder presenting with hypersomnia and low motivation
Narcolepsy with cataplexy caused by loss of hypocretin signalling
Obstructive sleep apnoea producing fragmented sleep and daytime somnolence
Focal epilepsy with atonic seizures and associated postictal confusion
Delayed sleep phase disorder with chronic insufficient sleep on weeknights

subtopic_detail: balancing the risk of refeeding against the risk of continued underfeeding in a severely malnourished adolescent
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 15-year-old girl with anorexia nervosa who has lost 16 kg over eight months. She is on day two of admission to a specialist adolescent unit with continuous cardiac monitoring.

She was started on a nutrition plan yesterday and her intake is being supervised. Overnight her heart rate fell to 38 beats per minute while asleep and she has had one episode of dizziness on standing. Her weight for height is 68 percent of expected. She has no oedema and no confusion. Her phosphate was 1.10 mmol/L on admission and is 0.72 mmol/L this morning, her magnesium has fallen from 0.88 to 0.71 mmol/L, and her potassium has fallen from 3.9 to 3.4 mmol/L. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia with a corrected QT interval of 440 ms and no arrhythmia. The dietitian asks whether the energy intake should be held or reduced.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 38/min asleep and 46/min awake, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg lying and 74/46 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 35.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Emaciated with lanugo hair, cool peripheries with capillary refill 3 seconds, no peripheral or sacral oedema, no crackles, Glasgow coma scale 15, no confusion or weakness
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate fallen from 1.10 to 0.72 mmol/L (0.80-1.50), magnesium fallen from 0.88 to 0.71 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), potassium fallen from 3.9 to 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), corrected QT interval 440 ms, glucose 3.6 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), thiamine given on admission

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her nutrition?

options.text: Halve the energy intake until the electrolytes return to the normal range
Cease enteral intake entirely and commence parenteral nutrition instead
Continue the current intake unchanged and recheck the electrolytes in 48 hours
Continue increasing energy intake with electrolyte replacement and daily monitoring
Maintain intake and give a fluid bolus to correct her postural blood pressure drop

subtopic_detail: continuing or withholding an effective antipsychotic when a stable woman with schizophrenia conceives
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 30-year-old woman with schizophrenia who has been well for three years on olanzapine 10 mg at night. She works part time, lives with her partner and has had no admission since her diagnosis at twenty four.

She tells you she is seven weeks pregnant and that the pregnancy is wanted and planned. She has read online that antipsychotics harm babies and has already missed four doses this week because she is frightened. She has no current psychotic symptoms, her sleep is normal and her insight is good. Her two previous relapses both followed her stopping medication, and the second involved a period of significant self neglect requiring inpatient care. Her booking bloods are normal and her body mass index is 26 kg/m2.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination shows euthymic mood, no hallucinations or delusions, no thought disorder, good insight, no extrapyramidal signs
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits, fasting glucose 4.9 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), beta human chorionic gonadotrophin consistent with seven weeks gestation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the current antipsychotic with added fetal growth surveillance
Stop the antipsychotic for the first trimester and restart it after organogenesis
Switch her to a first generation antipsychotic with longer established safety data
Halve the dose for the remainder of the pregnancy to reduce fetal exposure
Replace the antipsychotic with regular psychological therapy for the pregnancy

subtopic_detail: classifying recurrent disproportionate aggression that resolves completely between episodes in an otherwise law abiding adult
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 29-year-old man referred by his general practitioner after he punched a hole in a plasterboard wall when his internet connection dropped during a video call.

He describes roughly fortnightly episodes over the past three years in which he becomes enraged within seconds over something he later agrees was trivial, shouts, and sometimes throws or breaks an object. The episodes last under twenty minutes and he is remorseful and embarrassed afterwards. Between episodes his mood is stable and he is described by his partner as gentle. He has never been arrested, does not deceive people or take their belongings, has never harmed an animal, and had no behavioural difficulties at school. He drinks two beers on Fridays and uses no other substances. He has no head injury, no seizures and no memory gaps around the episodes.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination normal between episodes with euthymic mood, reactive affect, no psychotic phenomena, no cognitive impairment, no focal neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and urine drug screen all within normal limits, electroencephalogram reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Antisocial personality disorder with a predominantly aggressive presentation
Bipolar affective disorder with recurrent irritable hypomanic episodes occurring
Intermittent explosive disorder with recurrent impulsive aggressive outbursts
Borderline personality disorder with affective instability and anger dyscontrol
Focal epilepsy of temporal lobe origin presenting with episodic ictal aggression

subtopic_detail: distinguishing genuine autobiographical memory loss from feigned amnesia when a financial motive is present
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see a 44-year-old man brought to the emergency department by police after being found wandering in a coastal town three hundred kilometres from his home.

He cannot recall his name, his address or anything about his personal history, and he appears genuinely distressed by this. He is oriented to place and time, can tell you the date and the name of the prime minister, drove himself there and can operate his phone, read the newspaper and describe how to make a cup of tea. His wife arrives and tells you he had been served with bankruptcy papers the day before he disappeared and that his father died by suicide in similar financial circumstances. Computed tomography of his head is normal, his ethanol level is zero and his urine drug screen is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert and cooperative, distressed affect, no thought disorder or psychotic phenomena, cranial nerves and peripheral neurological examination normal, no head injury, Mini Mental State Examination 29 out of 30
data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography of the head normal, ethanol zero, urine drug screen negative, electrolytes, glucose, liver function, thyroid function and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Wernicke encephalopathy with confabulation from thiamine deficiency
Dissociative amnesia with dissociative fugue following overwhelming stress
Transient global amnesia with dense anterograde memory loss and repeated questioning
Malingered amnesia motivated by avoidance of impending bankruptcy proceedings
Non convulsive status epilepticus producing a prolonged postictal confusional state

subtopic_detail: establishing the nature of frequent prolonged events that have not responded to escalating anticonvulsant treatment
stem:
You are the neuropsychiatry registrar seeing a 24-year-old woman referred with events occurring up to four times a week for two years. She has been treated with three anticonvulsants at therapeutic doses without any reduction in frequency.

Her partner has recorded one on a phone. During the event she lies on the floor with her eyes tightly closed, her head turns rapidly from side to side, and her limbs move in an irregular asynchronous way that waxes and wanes over nine minutes. She resists having her eyelids opened. She has never been incontinent, has never bitten her tongue and has never been injured. Afterwards she is tearful but immediately oriented and can describe the room throughout. Her magnetic resonance imaging is normal, her routine interictal electroencephalograms have been normal, and her serum lactate taken twenty minutes after one event was normal.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal between events, normal gait and coordination, mental state shows anxious affect with no psychotic phenomena, no cognitive impairment
data_table.Investigations: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain normal, three routine interictal electroencephalograms normal, serum lactate normal twenty minutes after a witnessed event, electrolytes glucose and calcium within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Video electroencephalography telemetry to capture a typical event
Add a fourth anticonvulsant and reassess the frequency after three months
Repeat the magnetic resonance imaging using a dedicated epilepsy protocol
Measure serum prolactin immediately after the next witnessed event occurs
Arrange cardiac monitoring with a prolonged implantable loop recorder inserted

subtopic_detail: reconsidering a long standing anxiety label in a woman whose exhaustion follows social effort rather than preceding it
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 31-year-old woman referred after a third trial of a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor failed to help what has been treated as social anxiety disorder since she was nineteen.

She describes rehearsing conversations in advance, keeping a mental list of topics, and copying the facial expressions of colleagues so she appears normal. She says she is not frightened of being judged but finds the effort of appearing natural exhausting, and she sleeps for most of Saturday after a working week. She has an encyclopaedic knowledge of eighteenth century textiles and can talk about them at length. She reports that unexpected changes to plans leave her unable to function for the rest of the day, that certain clothing labels are unbearable against her skin, and that she has always counted steps when walking.

data_table.Examination: Limited spontaneous eye contact with effortful compensation, precise formal speech, mood euthymic, no psychotic phenomena, no compulsions performed to neutralise a feared outcome
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, thyroid function and iron studies within normal limits, previous trials of sertraline, escitalopram and venlafaxine each at adequate dose and duration without benefit

lead_in: What is the most likely explanation for her presentation?

options.text: Treatment resistant social anxiety disorder requiring augmentation of her medication
Obsessive compulsive disorder with counting compulsions and an intense special interest
Autism spectrum disorder with camouflaging that has delayed her diagnosis
Schizoid personality disorder with restricted affect and a preference for solitude
Persistent depressive disorder producing fatigue, low motivation and social withdrawal

subtopic_detail: identifying the disorder behind repeated presentations for infant reassurance when screening for low mood is negative
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29-year-old woman with her 10-week-old first baby. This is her fifth visit in three weeks, each time about a different symptom in the baby that has resolved by the time she arrives.

She describes checking the baby's breathing between eight and ten times each night and lying awake listening to the monitor even when the baby is asleep and settled. She has intrusive images of the baby stopping breathing that she finds horrifying and wholly unwanted, and she has never had any thought of harming the baby herself. She says her mood is fine, she enjoys the baby, she laughs with her partner and she looks forward to her mothers group. She is eating normally but is exhausted. Her Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score is 11, with the three anxiety items accounting for most of it and item 10 scored zero.

data_table.Examination: Appears tired but engaged, interacts warmly and responsively with the baby, mood euthymic with reactive affect, no psychotic phenomena, no thoughts of harm to self or the baby
data_table.Investigations: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale 11 with item 10 scored zero, full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function all within normal limits, baby thriving on the 50th centile with a normal examination

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Postnatal anxiety disorder with prominent checking and intrusive unwanted images
Postnatal depression that the screening tool has partially failed to capture
Postpartum psychosis with delusional beliefs about the baby's physical health
Factitious disorder imposed on another with fabricated symptoms in the infant
Normal adjustment to first time parenthood requiring reassurance and sleep support

subtopic_detail: the oral cover required when a depot antipsychotic is started, which differs between preparations
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 28-year-old man with schizophrenia who has had two relapses in three years, each following a period of stopping his tablets. He has been well for four months on oral aripiprazole 15 mg daily and has agreed to move to a monthly injection.

He tolerates the oral medicine without akathisia, sedation or movement problems, and his most recent metabolic screen was unremarkable. He lives with his parents, who prompt him with tablets, and he is returning to study next month. The first injection of aripiprazole 400 mg is given today in the clinic. He asks whether he can stop the tablets now that he has had the injection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No rigidity, tremor or abnormal involuntary movements, weight stable over four months, injection site normal
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose, lipids, full blood count, electrolytes and liver function all within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Aripiprazole 15 mg orally daily, aripiprazole 400 mg intramuscular given today

lead_in: What should you advise about his oral medicine?

options.text: Halve the oral dose today and stop it after the second injection next month
Continue the oral dose for three weeks, as required with the risperidone injection
Stop the oral dose today because the injection provides immediate therapeutic cover
Continue the oral dose for fourteen days after this injection and then stop it
Continue the oral dose indefinitely because injections alone rarely maintain remission

subtopic_detail: the interval required before an irreversible enzyme inhibitor can follow an antidepressant with an active metabolite
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 44-year-old woman with severe depression that has not responded to three adequate antidepressant trials. Your consultant has decided to move her to phenelzine and has asked you to organise the change.

She is currently taking fluoxetine 40 mg daily, which she has been on for eleven weeks with no benefit. She has no psychotic symptoms, is not suicidal, and lives with her husband who is supportive. She has no cardiac or renal disease, takes no other prescribed medicine and uses no over the counter preparations or herbal supplements. She has already been counselled about the dietary restrictions that go with the new medicine and is keen to start as soon as possible.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No tremor, no clonus, no hyperreflexia, no rigidity, mental state shows low mood with reactive affect and no psychosis
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function all within normal limits

lead_in: How should the change be made?

options.text: Switch to a two week course of sertraline first and then allow a two week washout
Cross taper the two medicines over ten days to avoid a period without treatment
Stop the fluoxetine and wait five weeks before the first dose of the new medicine
Stop the fluoxetine and wait two weeks before the first dose of the new medicine
Halve the fluoxetine for two weeks and then start the new medicine at a low dose

subtopic_detail: the monitoring schedule that must be arranged before a particular antidepressant is dispensed
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 38-year-old man with a first episode of moderate depression whose main complaints are early waking and daytime fatigue. He has previously stopped two antidepressants because of sexual dysfunction and asks specifically about agomelatine, which a colleague at work takes.

He drinks two standard drinks most evenings and has no history of hepatitis, jaundice or alcohol related liver disease. He takes no other medication, has no known allergies and does not use recreational drugs. His weight is stable and his examination is unremarkable. He is engaged with a psychologist and is not suicidal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No jaundice, no hepatomegaly, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, body mass index 25
data_table.Investigations: No blood tests performed to date

lead_in: What must you arrange if you prescribe this medicine?

options.text: No specific monitoring, with review at two weeks to assess response and tolerability
Liver function tests before starting and again at three, six, twelve and twenty four weeks
A full blood count before starting and weekly for the first eighteen weeks of treatment
Serum sodium before starting and again at two weeks, then every three months
An electrocardiogram before starting and again once the maintenance dose is reached

subtopic_detail: a low neutrophil count on clozapine in a patient whose baseline count was always at the lower limit
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 32-year-old man of West African descent with treatment resistant schizophrenia who has been on clozapine 400 mg daily for seven months with a very good response, having failed two previous antipsychotics.

His monitoring bloods today show a neutrophil count of 1.4 x10^9/L. Looking back through the record, his neutrophil counts have run between 1.5 and 1.9 x10^9/L at every check since before clozapine was started, and a full blood count taken during an admission four years ago showed a neutrophil count of 1.6. His total white cell count has always tracked at the lower end while his lymphocytes are normal. He is afebrile, has no sore throat, mouth ulcers or other infective symptoms, and feels well.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No oral ulceration, no pharyngeal inflammation, no lymphadenopathy, chest clear, no focus of infection
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 1.4 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), lymphocytes 2.1 x10^9/L (1.0-4.0), haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180), platelets 240 x10^9/L (150-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately and record it as a permanent contraindication for the future
Add lithium to raise the neutrophil count and continue the current clozapine dose
Refer to haematology to confirm a constitutional low count and apply modified thresholds
Halve the clozapine dose and repeat the full blood count in one week
Continue unchanged and repeat the count at the next scheduled monitoring interval

subtopic_detail: an analgesic bought over the counter that alters the handling of a narrow therapeutic index drug
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 46-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has been stable on lithium carbonate 750 mg at night for six years. She has come in about low back pain after moving house and mentions that she has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for the past ten days, bought from the supermarket.

Over the past four days she has felt nauseated, her hands have been shakier than usual, and she describes feeling unsteady on her feet. She has not vomited, has been drinking normally and has not had diarrhoea. She has had no recent dose change, no new prescribed medicines and no fevers. On examination she has a fine tremor that is coarser than her usual lithium tremor, and her gait is mildly unsteady with normal power and no focal signs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84/min, blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Coarse bilateral hand tremor, mild gait ataxia, normal power and reflexes, no clonus, no confusion, oriented and coherent
data_table.Investigations: No bloods taken yet today
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 750 mg orally at night, ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for ten days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Switch the ibuprofen to regular celecoxib, which does not interact with lithium
Refer her directly to the emergency department for consideration of haemodialysis
Continue both medicines and recheck the lithium level at her next routine appointment
Stop the ibuprofen and take an urgent lithium level with electrolytes and creatinine
Halve the lithium dose today and continue the ibuprofen until the back pain settles

subtopic_detail: separating the presence of mental illness from the capacity to refuse a specific medical treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to the surgical ward to see a 45-year-old man with schizophrenia who is refusing an appendicectomy. The surgical team has told you he lacks capacity because of his diagnosis and has asked you to authorise the operation under mental health legislation.

He has been on paliperidone for eight years and his last relapse was six years ago. He tells you he understands he has an infected appendix, that it may burst, and that this could kill him. He says he is refusing because his brother died under a general anaesthetic three years ago and he is frightened of the anaesthetic rather than the surgery. He repeats this account consistently and can explain the trade off he is making. He has no delusions about the surgical team, no hallucinations and no thought disorder on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98/min, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Right iliac fossa tenderness with guarding, mental state shows no delusions or hallucinations, speech coherent and goal directed, oriented to time place and person
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5), computed tomography showing an inflamed appendix without perforation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to the surgical team?

options.text: Advise the team to proceed once he is sedated for pain, as consent will then be simpler
Document that he retains capacity for this decision and that his refusal must be respected
Contact the guardianship board for an urgent substitute decision maker to be appointed
Increase his antipsychotic dose and reassess his capacity again in forty eight hours
Authorise the operation under mental health legislation given the risk to his life

subtopic_detail: choosing an antidepressant when a concurrent medicine depends on a hepatic enzyme for activation
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 52-year-old woman who finished treatment for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer eight months ago and now takes tamoxifen 20 mg daily. She describes two months of low mood, anhedonia and poor concentration that meet criteria for a moderate depressive episode, alongside troublesome hot flushes.

She has never taken an antidepressant. She has no suicidal thoughts and no psychotic symptoms. She has no cardiac disease, her blood pressure is normal, and she takes no other medication and no herbal preparations. She has already started with a psychologist and wants medication as well because the hot flushes are waking her several times a night.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mental state shows low mood with restricted affect, no psychomotor retardation, no psychosis, weight stable
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function all within normal limits

lead_in: Which antidepressant is the most appropriate choice?

options.text: Fluoxetine, which is well tolerated and can be given as a single morning dose
Venlafaxine, which has minimal effect on the enzyme that activates her other medicine
Paroxetine, which is effective for depression and also reduces vasomotor symptoms
Bupropion, which avoids sexual adverse effects and assists with fatigue and motivation
Sertraline, which is first line for depression and is widely used after cancer treatment

subtopic_detail: aggression confined to one care task in dementia, where the trigger rather than the illness explains it
stem:
You are the general practitioner asked by a residential aged care facility to prescribe something for a 79-year-old man with Alzheimer disease who has hit staff three times this month. The facility manager wants a regular antipsychotic started today.

The nursing notes show that every incident occurred during the morning shower, that all three involved the same two staff members, and that he is calm and cooperative at every other time of day including mealtimes and personal care in the evening. He has not been wandering, is sleeping through the night and has no hallucinations or persecutory beliefs described. He grimaces when his right shoulder is moved and has a documented rotator cuff problem. A urinalysis last week was negative and he is afebrile with no new medications.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 134/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Painful restricted right shoulder abduction, no delirium, attention preserved, no focal neurology, chest clear, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative last week, full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Donepezil 10 mg orally daily, paracetamol as required for pain

lead_in: What should you recommend?

options.text: Regular analgesia with a changed showering routine and review after two weeks
Prescribe as required oxazepam for staff to give before the morning shower
Increase the donepezil dose to address the behavioural symptoms of his dementia
Start regular risperidone at a low dose and review the response in four weeks
Send a urine sample and treat for infection while awaiting the culture result

subtopic_detail: choosing relapse prevention pharmacotherapy when the organ that clears one option is already damaged
stem:
You are the addiction medicine registrar seeing a 54-year-old man on day nine of an inpatient admission who completed alcohol withdrawal management a week ago and wants medication to help him stay abstinent after discharge. He was drinking about fifteen standard drinks daily for twelve years.

He has established cirrhosis with a previous episode of ascites, and his most recent hepatic imaging showed a nodular liver with splenomegaly. He has no encephalopathy now and is fully oriented. His renal function is normal. He takes no opioids and has no chronic pain. He is motivated, has a supportive partner, has been linked with a community drug and alcohol service, and his aim is complete abstinence rather than reduced drinking.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Spider naevi and palmar erythema, no ascites clinically, no asterixis, oriented with normal attention, no jaundice today
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 34 micromol/L (less than 20), albumin 29 g/L (35-50), international normalised ratio 1.5 (0.8-1.2), alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L (less than 40), creatinine 74 micromol/L (60-110)
data_table.Medications: Thiamine 300 mg orally daily, no other regular medicines

lead_in: Which relapse prevention medicine should you start?

options.text: Disulfiram, supervised by his partner, given his stated goal of complete abstinence
No medicine, with counselling and community follow up arranged as the whole plan
Naltrexone, which reduces heavy drinking days and is generally better tolerated
Acamprosate, with the dose set by body weight and renal function checked beforehand
Baclofen at a low dose, titrated upward according to his response over four weeks

subtopic_detail: the timing that determines whether the first dose relieves withdrawal or precipitates it
stem:
You are the registrar at a community drug and alcohol service starting a 29-year-old man on buprenorphine with naloxone for heroin dependence. He has been injecting about half a gram daily for four years and has agreed to opioid treatment after a friend died of an overdose.

He arrives at 9 am having used heroin at 7 am this morning, saying he wanted to be comfortable for the appointment. He denies methadone or other long-acting opioid use. He is not sweating, his pupils are small, he has no yawning, gooseflesh, abdominal cramps, rhinorrhoea or muscle aches, and he is comfortable sitting in the chair. His urine drug screen is positive for opioids only, and his hepatitis and human immunodeficiency virus screening is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pupils 2 mm and reactive, skin dry and warm, no piloerection, no rhinorrhoea, no tremor, alert and comfortable
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for opioids only, liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What should you do now?

options.text: Delay the first dose until objective withdrawal features are present, reviewing him later today
Start methadone today instead, since the recent heroin use makes it the safer option
Admit him for a naltrexone implant instead, given his high risk of fatal overdose
Give the first dose now with an antiemetic and clonidine to cover any reaction
Give a reduced first dose now and repeat it in four hours if he tolerates it

subtopic_detail: Restarting clozapine for a man who stopped taking it for three days while unwell at home
stem:
A 38-year-old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia attends your community mental health clinic. He has taken clozapine 400 mg at night for six years with good symptom control and no admissions in that time.

He had a bout of vomiting and diarrhoea over the weekend and did not take any clozapine on Saturday, Sunday or Monday. He restarted his usual night time dose last night of his own accord and now feels lightheaded on standing. He has no fever, no chest pain and no constipation, and his mental state is unchanged with no return of hallucinations. His full blood count today is normal and his observations show a postural drop in blood pressure.
