data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 102/62 mmHg lying with a fall to 84/50 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 4.1 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), C-reactive protein within normal limits
data_table.Medication: Clozapine 400 mg nightly for six years, no doses taken Saturday to Monday, full dose resumed last night

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his clozapine?

options.text: Continue the current dose and monitor his blood pressure closely over the next few days
Cease the current dose and retitrate from 12.5 mg daily using the standard escalation schedule
Halve the current dose to 200 mg nightly and increase back to 400 mg over the next week
Cease clozapine permanently and commence olanzapine at an equivalent antipsychotic dose
Continue the current dose and add fludrocortisone to manage the postural blood pressure drop

subtopic_detail: Timing of the first buprenorphine dose for a man who last used a long acting opioid the previous evening
stem:
A 34-year-old man attends your addiction medicine clinic wanting to start opioid replacement treatment. He has been using illicitly obtained slow release oral morphine and last took a dose at 8 pm yesterday, about fourteen hours ago.

He is keen to take his first dose immediately and is frustrated at the suggestion of waiting. On examination he is mildly anxious and restless with a pulse rate of 92/min, but his pupils are mid-sized rather than dilated, he has no sweating, no gooseflesh, no lacrimation and no yawning. His objective withdrawal score is 5. He has no other medical conditions and takes no other sedating medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Mildly anxious and restless, mid-sized pupils, no sweating, gooseflesh, lacrimation or yawning
data_table.Assessment: Objective opioid withdrawal score 5, last slow release morphine dose fourteen hours ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to his first dose?

options.text: Give the first dose now, since fourteen hours since his last use is a sufficient interval
Give the first dose now with an antiemetic and clonidine to cover any withdrawal symptoms
Wait until his objective withdrawal features score in the moderate range before the first dose
Start methadone today instead and reconsider transferring him to buprenorphine in a month
Give naloxone first to clear the receptor and then start buprenorphine an hour afterwards

subtopic_detail: Prevention of further seizures in a man who had a witnessed fit thirty hours after his last drink
stem:
A 52-year-old man is admitted under your team after a witnessed generalised seizure at home. He drinks about 20 standard drinks daily and his last drink was thirty hours before the seizure, having stopped because he ran out of money.

He has no history of epilepsy and has never had a seizure before. He is now alert and oriented with a mild tremor of the outstretched hands and is sweating lightly. His computed tomography brain scan is normal and there is no head injury. His electrolytes, glucose and magnesium are within normal limits, and his withdrawal scale score is 12.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 106/min, blood pressure 156/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented, mild tremor of outstretched hands, light sweating, no focal neurological signs, no head injury
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes glucose and magnesium within normal limits, computed tomography brain normal, withdrawal scale score 12

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment to prevent further seizures?

options.text: A loading regimen of oral phenytoin with parenteral thiamine given before any glucose
A loading regimen of oral carbamazepine with parenteral thiamine given before any glucose
Oral haloperidol as required with parenteral thiamine given before any glucose
A loading regimen of oral diazepam with parenteral thiamine given before any glucose
Symptom triggered oral diazepam only when his withdrawal scale score exceeds 15

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing a primary psychotic illness from a substance related one in a man with psychosis persisting a month after stopping methamphetamine
stem:
A 25-year-old man is reviewed on your inpatient unit. He was admitted five weeks ago with persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations after heavy daily methamphetamine use over the preceding six months.

He has been in hospital throughout with supervised urine drug screens that have been negative for four weeks. He was started on olanzapine on admission and his agitation settled within days, but he continues to describe a belief that a neighbour is transmitting messages about him, and he still hears two voices commenting on his actions. His family mention that in the year before he started using, he had withdrawn from friends, stopped attending TAFE and spent most of his time alone in his room. He has no fever, no confusion and a normal neurological examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Persecutory delusion and third person auditory hallucinations persisting, no confusion, no fluctuation in conscious state, normal neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: Supervised urine drug screens negative for four weeks, full blood count electrolytes and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the antipsychotic now, since his symptoms will resolve with continued abstinence alone
Record a firm diagnosis of schizophrenia now and counsel him that treatment will be lifelong
Switch to clozapine now, given that his symptoms have not resolved after five weeks of treatment
Continue the antipsychotic and reassess the diagnosis after a longer period of abstinence
Arrange lumbar puncture and autoimmune encephalitis antibody testing before altering treatment

subtopic_detail: Mutism with waxy limb posturing and reduced oral intake in a young woman with known bipolar disorder
stem:
A 22-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is admitted to your unit after four days of progressive withdrawal. She has not spoken since yesterday and has taken almost no food or fluid for two days.

She was started on olanzapine eight days ago by her general practitioner for elevated mood and reduced sleep. On examination she is awake with her eyes open and follows you around the room with her gaze, but does not respond to questions. When you lift her arm it remains in the position you leave it in. She resists passive eye opening and repeats your words back to you intermittently. She has no fever, her muscle tone is not rigid, and her creatine kinase is mildly raised.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Mutism, waxy flexibility with limbs retained in imposed positions, negativism, echolalia, no rigidity, no autonomic instability
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 420 U/L (<200), white cell count 8.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, computed tomography brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Increase the olanzapine dose and observe her response over the next forty eight hours
Commence dantrolene with active cooling and transfer her to the intensive care unit
Refer urgently for electroconvulsive therapy before trying any pharmacological treatment
Give a parenteral lorazepam challenge and withhold the antipsychotic while she is observed
Arrange lumbar puncture and electroencephalography before starting any specific treatment

subtopic_detail: Polyuria and thirst with a normal lithium level in a man treated with lithium for twelve years
stem:
A 49-year-old man attends your clinic reporting that he now passes urine four or five times each night and drinks constantly through the day. He has taken lithium for twelve years for bipolar I disorder and his mood has been stable throughout.

He has no polyphagia and has lost no weight. His fasting glucose and glycated haemoglobin are normal, and his morning lithium level taken twelve hours after his dose is within the therapeutic range. His sodium is at the upper limit of normal and his creatinine has risen slightly compared with results from two years ago. He is passing large volumes of dilute urine and a urine dipstick shows no glucose, protein or blood.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 134/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 145 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 108 micromol/L (60-110), fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), glycated haemoglobin 5.3% (<6.0), lithium level within the therapeutic range
data_table.Urine: Large volumes of dilute urine, dipstick negative for glucose protein and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure him that the symptoms are benign, since his lithium level is within range
Measure paired serum and urine osmolality and involve the renal team in his care
Start a fluid restriction of 1.5 litres daily and review his symptoms in four weeks
Add desmopressin and continue the lithium at the current dose with monthly review
Arrange an oral glucose tolerance test and a water deprivation test on the same day

subtopic_detail: Choice of pharmacotherapy for a depressive episode in a man with an established diagnosis of bipolar disorder
stem:
A 36-year-old man attends your clinic with eight weeks of low mood, anhedonia, hypersomnia and poor concentration that have caused him to take leave from work. He has a documented diagnosis of bipolar I disorder following a manic episode requiring admission four years ago.

He stopped his mood stabiliser eighteen months ago when he felt well and has taken nothing since. He denies any current elevated mood, reduced need for sleep or racing thoughts, and there are no psychotic features. He has passive thoughts that he would rather not be here but no plan and no intent, and he agrees to a safety plan with his partner present. His thyroid function and full blood count are normal and he does not use alcohol or other drugs.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Depressed mood with psychomotor slowing, no elevated mood or pressured speech, no psychotic features, passive thoughts of not wanting to be here without plan or intent
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function and full blood count within normal limits, no substance use

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Sertraline as monotherapy, titrated to an effective dose with review of his mood weekly
Venlafaxine as monotherapy, titrated to an effective dose with review of his mood weekly
Lithium at a low starting dose with review of his mood and a level taken weekly
Psychological therapy alone with review of his mood weekly and no medication started
Quetiapine as monotherapy, titrated to an effective dose with review of his mood weekly

subtopic_detail: Behavioural disturbance with visual hallucinations and marked motor slowing in an older man with fluctuating cognition
stem:
A 78-year-old man is brought to your clinic by his wife because he has become distressed and occasionally aggressive in the evenings over the past two months. She describes him seeing small children in the lounge room who are not there, and says these episodes do not frighten him.

She reports his alertness varies markedly, with some days when he is sharp and others when he stares into space for long periods. He has become slower to move and has fallen twice, and he acts out his dreams at night with kicking and shouting. His examination shows symmetrical bradykinesia with mild rigidity and no tremor. His urine is clear, his electrolytes and thyroid function are normal, and his medication list contains no anticholinergic agents.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 138/80 mmHg lying with a fall to 118/68 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical bradykinesia with mild rigidity, no resting tremor, fluctuating attention, formed visual hallucinations without fear
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes thyroid function and full blood count within normal limits, urine dipstick clear, no anticholinergic medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management of his behavioural symptoms?

options.text: Non-pharmacological measures with review of contributing medications and carer support
Low dose oral risperidone at night with review of his symptoms after two weeks
Low dose oral haloperidol as required with review of his symptoms after two weeks
Oral diazepam at night with review of his symptoms and falls risk after two weeks
Oral levodopa titrated upwards with review of his motor and behavioural symptoms fortnightly

subtopic_detail: Tremor and confusion at a lithium level reported as within range in a woman recently started on two antihypertensives, with the sample taken six hours after her dose
stem:
A 68-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is brought to your emergency department by her son with four days of worsening unsteadiness, slurred speech and intermittent confusion. She has taken lithium carbonate 500 mg twice daily for nine years with levels consistently between 0.6 and 0.8 mmol/L.

Three weeks ago her general practitioner started perindopril and hydrochlorothiazide for newly diagnosed hypertension. She has had no vomiting or diarrhoea and no fever. Her son took her to a collection centre on the way in, where a lithium level was drawn at 2 pm; she took her morning dose at 8 am. That level is reported as 1.1 mmol/L. On examination she has a coarse tremor, dysarthria, ataxia and intermittent myoclonic jerks, and she is drowsy but rousable with no neck stiffness.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor, dysarthria, ataxia, intermittent myoclonic jerks, drowsy but rousable, no neck stiffness, no focal signs
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 1.1 mmol/L drawn six hours after the morning dose, creatinine 148 micromol/L (45-90) up from 72 two months ago, sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), estimated glomerular filtration rate 32 mL/min/1.73m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Withhold the next lithium dose, observe overnight and repeat the level in the morning
Give activated charcoal and commence whole bowel irrigation to reduce ongoing absorption
Repeat the level timed correctly, start intravenous sodium chloride and discuss dialysis with the renal team
Continue the lithium at a reduced dose, cease the thiazide and arrange review in one week
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate to enhance urinary elimination and repeat the level in six hours

subtopic_detail: Electrolyte monitoring and supplementation in the first week of nutritional restoration for a severely underweight adolescent
stem:
A 16-year-old girl is admitted under your team with anorexia nervosa. She has eaten almost nothing for eleven days and her weight has fallen to a body mass index of 13 kg/m2.

Her admission bloods show normal electrolytes including a phosphate at the lower end of the reference range. Her pulse is 42/min and she has a postural drop in blood pressure, and her electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia with a corrected QT interval of 440 ms. The dietitian proposes commencing nutritional restoration today and asks you to write the monitoring and supplementation plan for the first week.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 42/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg lying with a fall to 76/48 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 35.8 °C
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate 0.82 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), magnesium 0.75 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), corrected QT interval 440 ms, albumin 36 g/L (35-50)
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 13 kg/m2, cool peripheries, lanugo hair, no oedema

lead_in: What monitoring and supplementation plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Daily phosphate measurement with supplementation begun once the level falls below range
Daily phosphate measurement with supplementation begun before the level falls below range
Twice weekly phosphate measurement with supplementation begun once the level falls below range
Delay all nutritional restoration for 72 hours while daily electrolytes are observed for stability
Daily phosphate measurement with a high carbohydrate feeding regimen to restore weight rapidly

subtopic_detail: Baseline assessment required before a first stimulant prescription in an adult newly diagnosed with attention deficit disorder
stem:
A 29-year-old man attends your practice having been newly diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder by a psychiatrist, who has recommended a trial of a stimulant and asked you to complete the baseline assessment.

He has lifelong difficulty sustaining attention and organising tasks, documented from school reports, and he has lost two jobs because of missed deadlines. He drinks alcohol occasionally and uses no other substances. He tells you his father died suddenly at 44 while playing sport, and that the cause was never fully explained to the family. He has no chest pain, no palpitations and no history of syncope himself.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Normal heart sounds with no murmur, no signs of heart failure, normal peripheral pulses
data_table.History: Father died suddenly at 44 during exertion with no cause established, no personal syncope, chest pain or palpitations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before starting treatment?

options.text: Record his heart rate and blood pressure and commence the stimulant at a low dose
Arrange a urine drug screen and commence the stimulant once the result is confirmed negative
Commence atomoxetine instead, since it avoids any need for cardiac assessment beforehand
Arrange an electrocardiogram and cardiology assessment before the first stimulant dose
Arrange thyroid function tests and commence the stimulant once the results are within range

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing an expected bereavement reaction from a depressive episode five weeks after the death of a spouse
stem:
A 71-year-old woman is brought to your practice by her daughter five weeks after her husband of forty six years died of pancreatic cancer. Her daughter is worried that she is depressed and asks you to start an antidepressant.

She describes waves of sadness that come when she finds his belongings or hears a particular song, interspersed with periods where she can enjoy her grandchildren's visits and laugh with them. Her sleep is broken and her appetite is reduced, and she has lost 2 kg. She says she misses him unbearably and sometimes hears his voice calling her name as she falls asleep, which she finds comforting rather than frightening. She does not blame herself for his death, retains her sense of her own worth, and says she wants to be here for her grandchildren.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Tearful when speaking about her husband but able to be consoled and to engage warmly, no psychomotor retardation, normal cognition
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function and vitamin B12 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence an antidepressant now with review of her mood and tolerability in two weeks
Commence a hypnotic for the disturbed sleep with review of her mood and function in two weeks
Commence an antipsychotic at low dose to address the auditory experiences she has described
Refer urgently to the older persons mental health team for specialist assessment this week
Continue supportive review with practical bereavement support and no antidepressant at this stage

subtopic_detail: Matching alcohol relapse prevention pharmacotherapy to a goal of reduced drinking rather than abstinence
stem:
A 45-year-old carpenter attends your general practice asking for help with his drinking. He describes about ten standard drinks most evenings, morning shakiness that settles once he has a drink, and two failed attempts to cut down on his own.

He is clear that he does not want to stop completely at this stage but wants to get the amount down, and he will not consider an inpatient admission. He takes no regular medication, uses no opioids and has never injected drugs. His liver enzymes are mildly raised at twice the upper limit of normal with a normal bilirubin and normal synthetic function, and his renal function is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No stigmata of chronic liver disease, no asterixis, no peripheral neuropathy
data_table.Liver function: Alanine aminotransferase 82 U/L (less than 45), bilirubin 12 micromol/L (less than 20), albumin and international normalised ratio within normal limits
data_table.Other: Renal function within normal limits, no current opioid use, declines inpatient withdrawal

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy is most appropriate to offer him now?

options.text: Acamprosate started once he has completed a supervised withdrawal
Disulfiram with supervised dosing arranged through his pharmacy
Naltrexone started now while he continues to drink at a reduced level
Baclofen at high dose titrated against his reported craving levels
Topiramate titrated slowly as first line pharmacotherapy for craving

subtopic_detail: Adding a specific antagonist when serotonin toxicity fails to settle with benzodiazepines and cooling
stem:
You are the emergency registrar treating a 38-year-old man brought in agitated and shaking three hours after his usual evening medications. He takes sertraline for depression and was started on tramadol by a locum two days ago for back pain.

On examination he is restless and diaphoretic. His pupils are dilated, and when you dorsiflex each ankle you elicit sustained beating that is more marked in the legs than the arms. His reflexes are brisk throughout. Both offending drugs have been withheld, he has received two doses of intravenous diazepam and active surface cooling has been running for forty minutes, but his temperature and agitation have not improved.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 132/min, blood pressure 158/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Sustained inducible ankle clonus greater in the lower than upper limbs, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, diaphoresis, normal muscle bulk without rigidity of the trunk
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 620 U/L (less than 200), creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, paracetamol not detected
data_table.Treatment so far: Both serotonergic agents withheld, two doses of intravenous diazepam, active cooling for forty minutes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate addition to his treatment?

options.text: Dantrolene given intravenously and repeated according to response
Bromocriptine given orally with continued supportive measures
Further escalating doses of benzodiazepine as the sole treatment
Oral cyproheptadine alongside active cooling and benzodiazepines
Intravenous physostigmine with continuous cardiac monitoring

subtopic_detail: Recurrent vomiting with compulsive hot bathing in a daily cannabis user after negative investigation
stem:
A 24-year-old man presents to your practice after his fourth emergency department attendance this year with severe vomiting. Each episode lasts two or three days and then resolves completely, leaving him entirely well for weeks or months.

He volunteers that the only thing that settles him during an episode is standing under a shower as hot as he can bear, sometimes for an hour at a time, and that his family have complained about the water bill. He has smoked cannabis daily since he was eighteen and has cut down before without stopping. A gastroscopy, abdominal ultrasound and coeliac serology arranged after his second presentation were all reported as normal, and his electrolytes between episodes are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits between episodes
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, no organomegaly, well hydrated at today's review
data_table.Investigations: Gastroscopy, abdominal ultrasound and coeliac serology all reported as normal, electrolytes and liver function within normal limits
data_table.Substance history: Daily cannabis use for six years, no alcohol, no other drugs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Ondansetron at higher dose with admission for intravenous fluids
Proton pump inhibitor trial with repeat gastroscopy in three months
Amitriptyline as prophylaxis for a cyclical vomiting syndrome
Referral for gastric emptying studies before any further treatment
Advise cannabis cessation and offer topical capsaicin for episodes

subtopic_detail: Driving advice for an adult established on stimulant treatment for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
stem:
A 27-year-old delivery driver attends your general practice for a repeat prescription. He was diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder eighteen months ago and has been on a stable dose of lisdexamfetamine prescribed by a psychiatrist for a year.

He tells you his concentration at work has improved markedly and that he has had no near misses or infringements since starting treatment. Before treatment he had two minor collisions reversing and was often described as distractible at the wheel. He has no history of substance misuse, no cardiac symptoms and no other medical conditions. He has read online that he might lose his licence and is considering stopping the medication without telling his psychiatrist.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular examination unremarkable, no tremor, weight stable
data_table.Treatment: Lisdexamfetamine at a stable dose for twelve months under specialist review
data_table.Driving history: Two minor collisions before treatment, none since, no infringements

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice to give him?

options.text: Advise him to stop driving until the stimulant has been ceased
Advise him to take a drug holiday from the stimulant on days he drives
Continue the stimulant and document the fitness to drive discussion
Report him to the licensing authority without discussing it with him
Switch him to a non stimulant agent before he drives again

subtopic_detail: Feature that separates schizoaffective disorder from bipolar disorder with psychotic features
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 29-year-old man in the community clinic. Over three years he has had two admissions with elevated mood, reduced sleep and grandiose beliefs that he had been chosen to reform the banking system, and one prolonged period of low mood.

His case manager has kept a daily mood chart. It shows that over the past eight months he has had two stretches of six to eight weeks in which his mood ratings, sleep and activity were all within his normal range. His mother reports that during those same stretches he continued to hear two voices commenting on his actions and remained convinced that his neighbours were reporting on him to a government agency. His urine drug screens have been negative throughout and his thyroid function is within normal limits.

data_table.Mood chart: Two periods of six to eight weeks with mood, sleep and activity ratings within his normal range
data_table.Mental state during euthymic periods: Persistent second person auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screens negative on repeated testing, thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.History: Two manic admissions and one depressive episode over three years

lead_in: Which feature best supports a diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder rather than bipolar disorder with psychotic features?

options.text: Grandiose delusions occurring during his periods of elevated mood
Delusions and hallucinations persisting while his mood was euthymic
A family history of bipolar disorder in his mother and maternal uncle
Poor response of his psychotic symptoms to lithium used on its own
Onset of his first psychotic episode in his early twenties at university

subtopic_detail: Correcting severe hyponatraemia with seizures after recreational drug use and excessive water intake
stem:
You are the emergency registrar receiving a 19-year-old woman brought in by ambulance from a music festival. Her friends say she took a tablet from someone in the crowd about six hours ago and then drank bottle after bottle of water because she had heard that overheating was the danger.

She became confused over the last hour and had a witnessed generalised seizure lasting ninety seconds in the ambulance, which terminated without treatment. On arrival she is drowsy and disoriented, with no focal neurological signs. Her capillary glucose is normal and her temperature is normal. Her initial venous blood gas and electrolytes have just returned.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy and disoriented, no focal neurological deficit, no neck stiffness, no rigidity or clonus
data_table.Biochemistry: Sodium 118 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), creatinine within normal limits, serum osmolality low
data_table.Other: Capillary glucose within normal limits, creatine kinase 340 U/L (less than 200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Fluid restriction alone with hourly neurological observations
Rapid infusion of two litres of normal saline over two hours
Intravenous five per cent dextrose to replace the free water deficit
Hypertonic saline in small boluses titrated to seizure control
Oral sodium chloride tablets with repeated biochemical monitoring

subtopic_detail: Advising on breastfeeding for a woman who has remained on lithium through pregnancy
stem:
You are the perinatal psychiatry registrar asked to review a 33-year-old woman on the postnatal ward on day 2 after the birth of her first baby. She has bipolar I disorder and remained on lithium throughout the pregnancy after a careful antenatal discussion, with levels monitored monthly and a normal fetal cardiac scan.

Her baby was born at 39 weeks, weighs 3.4 kg, is feeding well and has been examined as normal by the paediatric team. She very much wants to breastfeed. A midwife has told her she will have to use formula because her medication is dangerous, and she is distressed by this. She has a supportive partner, her mother is staying for a month, and she has a community perinatal nurse allocated.

data_table.Maternal bloods: Serum lithium 0.62 mmol/L (0.6-1.0), renal and thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Infant: Born at 39 weeks, birthweight 3.4 kg, newborn examination normal, feeding well
data_table.Support: Partner present, mother staying one month, community perinatal nurse allocated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about feeding?

options.text: Advise formula feeding because lithium is absolutely contraindicated
Support breastfeeding with no additional monitoring of the baby
Support breastfeeding with scheduled infant lithium and renal checks
Switch her to sodium valproate so that she can breastfeed safely
Stop the lithium for the duration of breastfeeding and restart later

subtopic_detail: Managing attenuated psychotic symptoms with preserved insight in a young person at ultra high risk
stem:
An 18-year-old man is brought to your youth mental health service by his mother, who is worried he has withdrawn from friends and dropped out of his first semester at university.

Over six months he has had increasing moments of feeling that strangers on the train are paying particular attention to him, and twice a week he hears someone call his name when no one is there. When you ask him directly, he says he knows these are probably his mind playing tricks and that he can talk himself out of them, though they frighten him at the time. He has no fixed beliefs he will defend, and he holds no conviction that anyone intends him harm. His father has schizophrenia. His urine drug screen is negative and his physical examination and bloods are unremarkable.

data_table.Mental state: Attenuated perceptual disturbance and ideas of reference with retained insight, no fixed delusions, no formal thought disorder, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Function: Withdrawal from peers, discontinued university course, social and occupational decline over six months
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, full blood count, renal, liver and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start a low dose atypical antipsychotic and review in four weeks
Cognitive behavioural therapy with scheduled review for transition
Start an antidepressant and review the psychotic symptoms later
Reassure and discharge with advice to return if symptoms worsen
Admit to an inpatient unit for observation and diagnostic clarity

subtopic_detail: First line approach to hyperactive delirium with identifiable reversible contributors after surgery
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to an orthopaedic ward at 11 pm about an 82-year-old man who is two days post hemiarthroplasty for a fractured neck of femur. The nursing staff say he is trying to climb out of bed and has pulled at his drip twice.

His daughter, who is at the bedside, says he was fully independent and sharp before the fall. His attention fluctuates through your assessment and he drifts off mid sentence, though he settles when she speaks to him. He has not opened his bowels since admission and a bladder scan shows a residual volume of 620 mL. He has been receiving regular oxycodone. He is afebrile, his chest is clear, and his electrolytes and inflammatory markers are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 138/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Cognition: Fluctuating attention with disorganised thinking, acute change from his documented baseline
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, abdomen distended, bladder scan residual 620 mL, no bowel action since admission
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, renal function, calcium, full blood count and inflammatory markers all within normal limits
data_table.Medication: Regular oxycodone since surgery, no anticholinergic agents

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Treat the reversible causes with orientation and nursing measures first
Start regular oral haloperidol and continue it until discharge home
Start a regular benzodiazepine at night to settle him and aid sleep
Apply physical restraints overnight to prevent him pulling at lines
Arrange computed tomography of the brain before any other action

subtopic_detail: Disposition after opioid reversal when the ingested agent has a longer duration than the antagonist
stem:
You are the emergency registrar receiving a 28-year-old man found unresponsive by his housemate. The ambulance crew recorded a respiratory rate of 6 per minute with pinpoint pupils and gave intramuscular naloxone, after which he woke rapidly.

He is now alert, orientated and irritable, and he wants to leave immediately. His housemate hands you an empty bottle from a community pharmacy dosing program and says he drank what was left of a friend's take home dose about three hours before he was found. His observations are currently normal and he has no focal neurological signs. His paracetamol level is undetectable and his electrocardiogram shows no conduction abnormality.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated, pupils 4 mm and reactive, no focal neurological deficit, chest clear
data_table.Ingestion history: Ingested another person's take home dose from an opioid dosing program about three hours before being found
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol undetectable, electrocardiogram shows normal intervals, electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Discharge him now that he is alert with normal observations
Give a further naloxone dose and then discharge him from the department
Admit him under the mental health act for involuntary observation
Observe with a naloxone infusion as the opioid outlasts the antagonist
Discharge with take home naloxone and no period of observation

subtopic_detail: Abdominal distension with absent bowel sounds in a patient established on clozapine
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on call asked to review a 38-year-old man on the inpatient unit who has taken clozapine for three years with good control of previously treatment resistant symptoms.

He has not opened his bowels for six days and has vomited twice this afternoon. He tells you his stomach feels tight and that he has been off his food since yesterday. On examination his abdomen is distended and tympanitic with generalised mild tenderness, and you cannot hear any bowel sounds after listening for a full minute. His neutrophil count from this week's routine monitoring is within normal limits, as is his temperature, and his most recent clozapine level was in the usual therapeutic range.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 106/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen distended and tympanitic, generalised mild tenderness, absent bowel sounds, no guarding
data_table.Bowel history: No bowel action for six days, two episodes of vomiting today, reduced oral intake
data_table.Monitoring bloods: Neutrophils within normal limits on routine weekly monitoring, clozapine level within the therapeutic range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Repeat the full blood count urgently as this suggests agranulocytosis
Reassure and prescribe a stool softener with review in one week
Cease the clozapine and observe without any further investigation
Arrange an urgent echocardiogram and troponin for possible myocarditis
Arrange urgent abdominal imaging and treat the hypomotility aggressively

subtopic_detail: Managing antipsychotic induced hyperprolactinaemia in a young woman wanting to preserve treatment
stem:
A 26-year-old woman with schizophrenia attends your community clinic. She has been well on risperidone for two years, works full time and is keen not to lose the stability she has achieved.

Her periods stopped about eight months ago and she has noticed milky discharge from both breasts. She finds this distressing and has started missing doses because of it. She is not pregnant on repeated testing and is not breastfeeding. She has no headaches and no visual symptoms, and her visual fields are full to confrontation. She takes no other medication, and her thyroid function and renal function are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bilateral galactorrhoea on expression, visual fields full to confrontation, no features of acromegaly
data_table.Investigations: Serum prolactin 1840 mIU/L (less than 500), pregnancy test negative on repeat, thyroid and renal function within normal limits
data_table.Medication: Risperidone for two years, no other prescribed or over the counter medication
data_table.Adherence: Recently intermittent because of the symptoms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Add a dopamine agonist while continuing the current antipsychotic
Arrange pituitary imaging before making any change to her treatment
Stop all antipsychotic treatment and monitor her mental state closely
Add the combined oral contraceptive pill and continue the risperidone
Switch to aripiprazole after excluding other causes of the elevation

subtopic_detail: Agitation and tachycardia after using a synthetic cannabinoid product
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 19-year-old man brought in by his housemates two hours ago. They say he smoked something he bought online that was sold as a herbal blend, and that within twenty minutes he was pacing, shouting and saying the walls were closing in.

He is agitated and difficult to redirect but is not threatening staff. He has no prior psychiatric history and no regular medication. A urine drug screen is negative for cannabis, amphetamines, opioids, benzodiazepines and cocaine. His housemates say he smokes ordinary cannabis most weekends without anything like this happening.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 132 beats per minute, blood pressure 158/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Agitated and pacing, mydriasis, tremor, no rigidity, no clonus, no focal neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative across the standard panel, electrocardiogram sinus tachycardia with a QTc of 420 ms, creatine kinase 320 U/L (less than 200), sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), blood glucose 6.1 mmol/L
data_table.Collateral: Regular weekend cannabis use with no previous psychotic symptoms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Give intramuscular haloperidol and admit him to the ward
Give oral diazepam and nurse him in a low stimulus area
Give oral propranolol to control his pulse and blood pressure
Discharge him now because the drug screen was entirely negative
Start olanzapine and refer him to the mental health team today

subtopic_detail: Urinary frequency and suprapubic pain in a regular ketamine user
stem:
A 24-year-old woman attends your general practice with eight months of passing urine every half hour during the day and burning pain above her pubic bone that eases briefly after she goes.

She has been treated with three courses of trimethoprim by different doctors for presumed urinary tract infection, each time without lasting benefit. All three midstream urine cultures were sterile. She has no fever, no vaginal discharge and no flank pain. When you ask about substance use she tells you she has used ketamine three or four nights a week for about two years. Her renal function is normal and a pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Suprapubic tenderness, no loin tenderness, no vaginal discharge, abdomen otherwise soft
data_table.Investigations: Three midstream urine cultures sterile, urinalysis shows microscopic haematuria without nitrites, creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), sexually transmitted infection screen negative, pregnancy test negative
data_table.Substance history: Ketamine three to four nights weekly for two years, no injecting, occasional alcohol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a longer course of trimethoprim and repeat the culture
Start an anticholinergic bladder agent and review in three months
Advise ketamine cessation and refer her to a urology service
Refer to a sexual health clinic for further infection screening
Reassure her that the symptoms are functional and review in a year

subtopic_detail: Persistent psychotic symptoms two months after stopping methamphetamine
stem:
A 23-year-old man is reviewed in your community mental health clinic. He was admitted ten weeks ago with persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations after several months of daily methamphetamine use, and was started on an antipsychotic.

He has been in a residential rehabilitation program since discharge with supervised random urine testing, and every sample over the past eight weeks has been negative for amphetamines and all other substances. He remains convinced that a criminal group has marked him for death and still hears two voices discussing him during the day. His affect is now blunted and he has withdrawn from the program's group activities. He has no fever, no confusion and no fluctuation in his level of consciousness.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated, blunted affect, no confusion, no tremor, no neurological focal signs, no evidence of intoxication or withdrawal
data_table.Investigations: Eight weeks of supervised urine drug screens all negative, full blood count, renal function, liver function, thyroid function and B12 within normal limits
data_table.Symptom course: Persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations persisting throughout eight weeks of verified abstinence
data_table.Treatment: Antipsychotic commenced ten weeks ago and taken under supervision

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop the antipsychotic since the causative substance has been ceased
Continue the antipsychotic and reassess after a further six months
Repeat the urine screen using hair testing for covert ongoing use
Treat as a primary psychotic illness and continue the antipsychotic
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before any change

subtopic_detail: Starting a long acting injectable antipsychotic in a patient never exposed to that agent
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community team reviewing a 27-year-old man with schizophrenia who has had three relapses in two years, each following him stopping his oral medication.

He has agreed to a long-acting injectable antipsychotic and the team has selected an agent he has not taken before in any form. He has no known drug allergy, no cardiac history and a normal electrocardiogram. He is currently well, living with his parents, and taking no antipsychotic at present having stopped two weeks ago. His mother asks what happens if the new injection does not agree with him, given that it lasts a month.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No extrapyramidal signs, no abnormal involuntary movements, body mass index 24 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal function, liver function, fasting glucose and lipids all within normal limits, electrocardiogram with a QTc of 408 ms
data_table.Medication history: Three previous relapses after stopping oral treatment, no previous exposure to the selected agent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate step before giving the first injection?

options.text: Give the full loading dose and observe him for two hours
Start a prophylactic anticholinergic before the first injection
Repeat the electrocardiogram one week after the first injection
Arrange a community treatment order before starting the depot
Give a period of the oral form of the same agent first

subtopic_detail: Depressive episode in bipolar disorder with two previous manic episodes
stem:
A 35-year-old woman attends your community mental health clinic with six weeks of low mood, loss of interest, sleeping twelve hours a night and difficulty concentrating at work. She has bipolar disorder with two previous manic episodes requiring admission, the most recent four years ago.

She stopped her mood stabiliser eighteen months ago against advice when she felt well and has taken nothing since. She has no psychotic symptoms and no current suicidal intent, though she says she sometimes wishes she would not wake up. She is not pregnant and is using an intrauterine device. Her thyroid function, renal function and full blood count are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Psychomotor slowing, reactive affect, no psychotic features, no evidence of elevated mood or pressured speech
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, renal function, liver function and full blood count all within normal limits, pregnancy test negative
data_table.Medication history: Ceased mood stabiliser eighteen months ago, currently on no psychotropic medication
data_table.Risk: Passive thoughts of not wanting to wake, no plan, no intent, good social support

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Start quetiapine and review her response in two weeks
Start sertraline and review her response in two weeks
Start venlafaxine and review her response in two weeks
Start diazepam and review her response in two weeks
Offer psychotherapy alone and review her response in two weeks

subtopic_detail: Safety planning for a farmer with suicidal thoughts and firearms at home
stem:
A 48-year-old farmer attends your rural general practice at his wife's insistence. Three years of drought have left the property in serious debt and he has been sleeping poorly and drinking more than usual.

He tells you he has thought about shooting himself, most often in the early morning when he cannot sleep, but that he has not made any plan and does not want to die so much as he wants the situation to end. He has three licensed firearms in a locked cabinet in the shed and he alone holds the key. He has no psychiatric history and no previous attempt. He is willing to accept help and his wife is supportive and present.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Tired appearing, reactive affect, no psychotic features, no evidence of intoxication today
data_table.Risk assessment: Passive and intermittent suicidal thoughts with a considered method, no plan, no previous attempt, protective factors include his wife and willingness to engage
data_table.Substance use: Approximately 40 standard drinks per week, increased from 15 over the past year
data_table.Access to means: Three licensed firearms stored in a locked cabinet to which he holds the only key

lead_in: Which intervention is most likely to reduce his risk of dying by suicide?

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at low dose today
Arrange for the firearms to be removed from the property
Ask him to sign a written agreement not to harm himself
Refer him for cognitive behavioural therapy with a psychologist
Arrange involuntary admission to the nearest inpatient unit

subtopic_detail: Duration of antipsychotic treatment for persistent aggression in dementia
stem:
You are the registrar reviewing an 84-year-old woman in a residential aged care facility. She has moderate Alzheimer dementia and was started on risperidone eleven weeks ago after repeatedly striking care staff during personal care.

Staff report that the hitting stopped within three weeks and there have been no incidents for the past eight weeks. Pain, constipation and urinary infection were all excluded at the time and a behaviour support plan was put in place with changes to how personal care is delivered. She is now more drowsy in the afternoons and has had two falls in the past month without injury. Her family ask whether she needs to stay on the medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg lying and 106/64 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy in the afternoon, mild cogwheel rigidity at both wrists, unsteady on standing, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal function and calcium within normal limits, midstream urine negative, no new medication changes
data_table.Treatment: Risperidone for eleven weeks, no aggressive incidents for eight weeks, behaviour support plan in place

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her medication?

options.text: Continue the current dose and review her again in six months
Switch her to quetiapine to reduce the parkinsonian symptoms
Begin a gradual dose reduction with a view to withdrawal now
Add benzatropine to treat her rigidity and continue the risperidone
Stop the risperidone abruptly and observe her over the weekend

subtopic_detail: Opioid agonist treatment for a woman who conceives while stable on buprenorphine
stem:
A 28-year-old woman attends your addiction medicine clinic having just discovered she is seven weeks pregnant. She has been on buprenorphine for two years, has not used heroin in that time, works part time and has stable housing.

She is frightened that the medication will harm the baby and tells you she has already halved her own dose this week and is planning to come off it altogether before the birth. She has mild withdrawal symptoms today. She has hepatitis C antibodies with an undetectable viral load after treatment, and is not using alcohol, benzodiazepines or stimulants. Her partner is also on opioid agonist treatment and is supportive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mild lacrimation and yawning, piloerection, pupils 4 mm, no injection sites, no stigmata of chronic liver disease
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for buprenorphine only, hepatitis C ribonucleic acid undetectable, hepatitis B and human immunodeficiency virus negative, full blood count and liver function within normal limits
data_table.Treatment history: Buprenorphine for two years with no heroin use, self reduced dose this week

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her opioid agonist treatment?

options.text: Support a staged withdrawal to be completed by the third trimester
Switch her to methadone because it is better studied in pregnancy
Reduce her dose gradually to minimise neonatal abstinence syndrome
Return her to her previous effective dose and continue it
Change her to naltrexone once her withdrawal is fully complete

subtopic_detail: Confusion three weeks after starting an antidepressant in a woman of seventy nine
stem:
You are the registrar asked to review a 79-year-old woman brought to hospital by her daughter, who says her mother has become increasingly muddled over the past week, has been unsteady on her feet and had one fall.

Three weeks ago her general practitioner started sertraline for a depressive episode. She also takes an indapamide for hypertension, which she has been on for six years without problems. She has had no vomiting, no diarrhoea and no diuretic dose change. She is clinically euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes, no postural drop and no oedema. Her chest is clear, her urinalysis is negative and her temperature is normal. She has had no seizures and is rousable and orientated to person only.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg lying with no postural drop, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, orientated to person only, unsteady gait, euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes and no oedema, no focal neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), serum osmolality 248 mmol/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 420 mmol/kg, urine sodium 52 mmol/L, thyroid function and 9 am cortisol within normal limits, creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90)
data_table.Medication: Sertraline started three weeks ago, indapamide for six years without previous problem

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give hypertonic saline urgently to raise the sodium concentration
Give intravenous sodium chloride 0.9 percent at a maintenance rate
Cease the thiazide diuretic and continue the antidepressant unchanged
Increase the antidepressant dose to treat her worsening depression
Cease the antidepressant and restrict her free water intake

subtopic_detail: Falling phosphate on the third day of refeeding in severe anorexia nervosa
stem:
You are the medical registrar on a ward where a 19-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa was admitted three days ago with a body mass index of 12.8 kg/m2 after four months of minimal intake. Nasogastric feeding was started on admission.

On day three her phosphate has fallen from 1.1 to 0.52 mmol/L and her magnesium and potassium have also drifted down. She is alert, is not breathless, and her chest is clear. The nursing staff ask whether feeding should be stopped because of the abnormal results. Her mother, who is present, says she is terrified the feeding is hurting her. There is no peripheral oedema and no new confusion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 46 beats per minute, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Emaciated, alert and orientated, chest clear, no peripheral oedema, no asterixis, jugular venous pressure not elevated
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate 0.52 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 52 micromol/L (45-90), electrocardiogram with a QTc of 465 ms
data_table.Feeding: Nasogastric feeding commenced on admission three days ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Replace phosphate and continue feeding at the current rate
Stop the feeding until the phosphate returns to normal range
Increase the feeding rate to correct her nutrition more quickly
Change to parenteral nutrition to bypass the gastrointestinal tract
Give a fluid bolus and repeat the electrolytes in the morning

subtopic_detail: Persistent orofacial movements after eight years of antipsychotic treatment
stem:
A 58-year-old woman with schizophrenia attends your clinic. She has taken haloperidol for eight years and her psychotic symptoms have been well controlled for the last five.

Her daughter has noticed over the past year that her mother is constantly chewing and that her tongue pushes out of her mouth when she is watching television. The movements stop while she is talking and she is largely unaware of them. They are not relieved by anything and she does not feel an inner restlessness or an urge to move. There is no tremor, no rigidity and no bradykinesia. She has no family history of Huntington disease and her recent thyroid function and copper studies were normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Continuous chewing and lateral tongue movements at rest, tongue protrusion on distraction, no resting tremor, no cogwheel rigidity, normal gait, no chorea of the limbs
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, copper studies, full blood count and renal function all within normal limits
data_table.Medication history: Haloperidol for eight years, no anticholinergic medication, no recent dose change
data_table.Symptom character: No subjective restlessness, no urge to move, movements reduce during speech

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Add benzatropine and review her movements in four weeks
Switch to a lower potency agent and refer for specialist review
Increase the haloperidol dose to suppress the movements directly
Stop the haloperidol abruptly and observe her over the next month
Start propranolol and review her movements again in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Relapse in a NSW patient with a written advance care directive naming a preferred medication
stem: You are the registrar assessing a 34-year-old man in a NSW emergency department. He has schizoaffective disorder and relapsed with persecutory delusions and disorganised speech after stopping medication three weeks ago. He refuses admission and medication; a mental health certificate is being completed. His file holds an advance care directive made two years ago while well: he wishes to receive olanzapine and not haloperidol, after a severe dystonic reaction. He has no contraindication to olanzapine.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 bpm, BP 132/82 mmHg, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Investigations: Metabolic screen normal last month, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: How should his directive influence your prescribing?

options.text: Disregard it, because he now lacks capacity to consent
Treat with haloperidol, because a schedule overrides his wishes
Treat with olanzapine, as his advance care directive records
Ask his sister to choose which medication he is given
Defer all medication until he regains capacity to consent
